speechtext:
Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade
and Commerce): Mr. Speaker, on February 18 I indicated to the house that I hoped to be able to announce some interim payments by the Canadian wheat board before seeding. I am now in the position to make an announcement with respect to barley.
Effective today the initial payment for all grades of barley has been increased by 10 cents per bushel. Until today the initial payment for the basic grade of barley, No. 3, C.W. 6-row was 96 cents per bushel basis in store Fort William/Port Arthur. The new price for this grade is now $1.06 per bushel and initial payments for all other grades have been increased by the same amount.
Producers who delivered barley to the Canadian wheat board between August 1,
1954,	and the close of business on March 12,
1955,	will receive an adjustment payment of 10 cents per bushel. The wheat board expects to commence issuing cheques covering this payment during the first week in April.
During the period from August 1, 1954, to March 12, 1955, producers in the prairie provinces delivered about 80 million bushels of barley to the board and therefore the adjustment payment will amount to about $8 million. The higher initial payment is effective today at all country elevators and will apply on barley delivered by producers for the balance of the crop year.
This is the first of a series of payments which will be made to producers by the wheat board this spring. In a few days, I expect to announce an increase in the initial payment for oats and, later, the final payment on the 1953-54 wheat pool.

RADIOACTIVE MATERIALS
speechtext: Is any action being taken by the federal government to protect the health of people engaged in the use of radioactive materials?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: RADIOACTIVE MATERIALS
speechtext:
Yes. In order to ascertain the amount of radiation being received by radiation workers the occupational health division of the Department of National Health and Welfare established in 1951 a film monitoring service. This service was originally designed to protect people working with radioisotopes but it has been expanded so that it can be used by people working with X-rays. Noting the amount of exposure received by these workers enables the division to give advice to the many industries, hospitals, and other bodies taking advantage of this service on appropriate ways of providing radiation protection.
The occupational health division of the Department of National Health and Welfare also gives advice during the planning stages of all radioisotopes laboratories, in order that radioactive material can be handled safely. Recommendations are made as to the design of the laboratory, safe techniques for using the radioactive isotopes and safe methods of disposing of radioactive waste so that there is no danger of contamination of air or water supplies. Advice is given concerning the training of personnel who are proposing to use radioactive materials. This division is planning to provide training courses emphasizing the safe use of radiation.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. Si. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: CANADIAN FLAG
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Girard) put a question to me. I was unable to hear it distinctly enough to grasp its full import. Here it is, as reported on page 1928 of Hansard:
Has the Prime Minister read in yesterday's press an account of an address in which the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill) stated that the red ensign had been the official flag of this country since 1945 and would remain so until parliament had chosen another?
I must confess I have not read all the newspaper reports but I have read the text of the minister's speech. The minister summarized, in the very few words of the document, an order in council dated September 5, 1945, P.C. 5888, authorizing the use of the Canadian red ensign within and without the limits of Canada wherever it is desirable to fly a distinctive Canadian flag. Neither in the order in council nor in the minister's speech have I found the words "official flag".
The second part of the hon. member's question is as follows:
Could he also tell us whether the red ensign is the temporary flag of this country, to serve until such time as parliament has adopted a permanent one or its official flag, and whether it will remain so until parliament has designated another, as the minister has said?
The only answer I can give is to repeat that neither in the order in council nor in the minister's speech have I found the words "official flag". As for the rest of the question, well, this order in council is still in force and, as long as it so remains, it provides that it is the red ensign that should be flown as the distinctive national flag.
I am sending the hon. member a copy of the order in council dated September 5, 1945, together with a copy of the translation published at that time.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: BRITISH INDUSTRIES FAIR-REPORTED DISCONTINUANCE OF PARTICIPATION BY CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday last, before the orders of the day were called, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) asked a question concerning the discontinuance of Canadian government participation in the British industries fair.

The British industries fair, as the name suggests, is for the purpose of promoting the interests of United Kingdom industries. The commonwealth countries have been permitted to participate on a government basis only. We have reviewed our position from time to time, and have entertained some serious doubts for the last two or three years as to whether or not our participation was justified. We asked our representatives on the spot to make a close examination last year as to the results obtained, and I must confess that these were rather disappointing. In the circumstances, therefore, it was decided that Canada would not show at the exhibition this year. I understand that all other members of the commonwealth have decided to stay out this year for the same reasons as we did.
Arrangements have been made for Canadian participation at the British plastics exhibition to be held next June, and the lumbering and building products at the building exhibition in November, both of which will be in London.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: BRITISH INDUSTRIES FAIR-REPORTED DISCONTINUANCE OF PARTICIPATION BY CANADA
speechtext: I have a question arising out of his answer which I should like to direct to the minister. In view of the importance of extended trade with the United Kingdom and the extended sales which may be possible, will the minister not reconsider this, having regard to the number of years that Canada has been represented at these fairs, both at London and at Birmingham, and also remembering that there are ways in which we can place before the people at those fairs Canadian goods in precisely the same way that British manufacturers place before the people of Canada at trade fairs here the goods that they produce? While we wish economy, the cost, I think the minister will agree, is comparatively trivial in relation to the over-all amount of trade involved, if in fact there is any possibility of this fair encouraging the sale of Canadian goods in Britain at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: BRITISH INDUSTRIES FAIR-REPORTED DISCONTINUANCE OF PARTICIPATION BY CANADA
speechtext:
The Leader of the Opposition is under a misapprehension when he says we can show Canadian goods at the British industries fair. That is not permitted. We can simply put in a national exhibit indicating that Canada manufactures certain goods; but it is not an exhibit where Canadian goods can be shown.
The character of the British industries fair has changed within the last year or two. It was formerly sponsored by the British government. It is not so sponsored at the present time. It is sponsored by the British

industry, and all commonwealth countries have agreed that a simple national exhibit is not helpful to any of us at the present time. Where we can show Canadian goods we do participate in British fairs, as is the case with the plastic exhibition and the lumbering exhibition.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

speechtext:
It appears that the questions have terminated and we are about to embark upon the orders of the day. I do not want to single out any particular question which has been asked, but rather I shall refer to them all. I have had occasion to say that I was not favourably impressed by the questions that were being asked on the orders of the day and I have suggested to hon. members that they read citation 295 to be found on page 119 of Beauchesne's third edition. Perhaps they have and it may be that those who have were not the ones who have been asking questions today. I should like to read some of the paragraphs in this citation to those who have been asking questions today or who may be asking questions tomorrow and on following days. This reads:
In putting a question a member must confine himself to the narrowest limits.
In asking a question, observations which might lead to debate cannot be regarded as coming within the proper limits of a question.
The purpose of a question is to obtain information and not supply it to the house.
A number of examples are given of questions which in the past have been decided as not being proper to ask and I should like to cite some of these. I shall not quote them all because there are some 30 or 40.
A question oral or written must not:
(c)	multiply, with slight variations, a similar question on the same point.
(d)	repeat in substance a question already answered, or to which an answer has been refused.
(e)	inquire whether statements made in a newspaper are true.
(f)	contain an expression of opinion.
(j) be framed so as to suggest its own answer.
(w) raise a matter of policy too large to be dealt with in the limits of an answer to the question.
(bb) ask the government's opinion on matters of policy.
(cc) ask what advice a minister proposes to give crown, (but may ask what advice he has given).
(gg) seek information about matters which are in their nature secret, such as decisions or proceedings of cabinet, advice given to crown by law officers, etc.
I know that it may be said by some hon. members that if they were to adhere strictly to those rules it might be difficult for them to enjoy the interesting question and answer period before the orders of the day are called, but I would remind hon. members that unless

we intervene from time to time to ask hon. members to refrain from asking questions which are obviously out of order, this matter is simply going to get out of hand.
I should like hon. members to consider seriously whether in many cases they should not wait until a particular department is in supply to ask some of their questions. Questions should be of an urgent and national character. Whether a bridge or dock is to be erected in a certain locality in an hon. member's constituency is a question which I think could wait until the estimates are before the house.
With these words I ask hon. members to co-operate and I am looking forward to a very interesting question and answer period in the days to come.

The house resumed, from Friday, March 11, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. St. Laurent-Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Defence Production Act to increase the salary of the Minister of Defence Production from ten thousand dollars per annum to fifteen thousand and to repeal section 41 which provided for the expiry of the act on July 31, 1956.

maintopic: ASKING OF QUESTIONS ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this subject has been under discussion already and there might be almost some question in the minds of many hon. members as to the extent to which further discussion is necessary, particularly having regard to the fact that at this stage there is not much difference of opinion as to the principles which are really involved in the request being made to the house. It is not always that the words of the Minister of Defence Production, who is responsible for the administration of this department, find complete acceptance in this house, and yet I think there will be acceptance of the statement made by the minister as reported at page 1969 of Hansard of March 11 as follows:
In my opinion it is esssential, in view of the kind of world in which we are now living, that we have a Department of Defence Production staffed with experienced and efficient personnel and with the powers to perform its operations on a continuing basis.
I think every hon. member will be in agreement with that proposition. However, that is not everything that is before us. The measure that will be under consideration when the bill comes before us is one which embraces a very wide field of administrative responsibility. It is to that measure that the
Defence Production Act remarks have been directed and it is to that measure that I propose to direct my remarks now.
Why talk about this at this stage? If parliament is still a representative body where the voice of the people can be heard through their representatives it is essential that we talk about problems of this kind at the time when they come forward for consideration even though we may recognize that the decision will in the end be determined by the government, and by the party which supports it, with reasonably uniform acceptance of the position that the government puts forward.
Why should this be discussed at this time? We all recognize the need for a Department of Defence Production? We all recognize that this department should have the necessary authority to acquire the necessary materials which are essential and to direct the production of those things which can be used in our participation in the joint defence of freedom.
The reason this subject should be discussed now is to be found in the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) himself at the time this bill came before us on an earlier occasion as reported at page 836 of Hansard of March 2, 1951. The Prime Minister is reported as using these words:
It is proposed that the act would expire on July 31, 1956. There is no particular significance to this date, other than to recognize that some of the powers sought in this bill are special powers which should not be of a continuing nature.
There, Mr. Chairman, is the reason we should be discussing this subject now and' there is the reason I am placing before the members of this house the earnest proposal that at this stage the Prime Minister reconsider the decision to proceed with this measure without substantial amendments and redrafting and also that due consideration be given to the way in which the special powers which are not necessary can be deleted without in any way impairing the effectiveness of the measure for the purposes it is intended to carry out.
Surely it is not too much to ask at this stage that the Prime Minister himself from both his parliamentary and legal background consider the words he used at the time this bill was introduced. He should also be prepared to consider at this time the possibility of drafting an act with all the facilities required but with appropriate restraints.
Mr. Chairman, may I say at this point that in quoting the statement a few moments ago, I have quoted the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) relating to a measure introduced by the Prime
1986	HOUSE OF
Defence Production Act Minister which I assume the Prime Minister accepted as a correct proposition in relation to this matter. I would not wish any misunderstanding to arise out of that quotation. The measure was introduced by the Prime Minister and the words I quoted in support of the introduction of that measure are the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I might perhaps expect the Prime Minister himself would have used more restrictive words, although not because he has any thought of restricting the measure more than any other member of the government. I recognize that under the system of government solidarity there must be acceptance of the proposition which is put forward, but the Minister of Trade and Commerce, anxious to proceed with the activities of that department, might well be inclined to state a broader desire for power under the act and for its continuance than might the Prime Minister himself.
I do ask the Prime Minister to reconsider those words. When I say they are the words of the Prime Minister I feel certain the Prime Minister will not in any way question the fact that these words represent a statement of the government as to what was proposed at that time.
I notice the Prime Minister nods approval of my remark, as I felt sure he would, in regard to such a simple and basic proposition which was then placed before us.
Now, Mr. Chairman, it has been said that we are living in very serious times. I do not think there is an hon. member of this house who is not fully conscious of the seriousness of the times in which we are living. The government may be charged with the day to day responsibility for speaking on behalf of Canada in international affairs. However, every hon. member of this house, as a member of parliament and a representative of the people who sent him here, is fully conscious of the extremely serious circumstances surrounding us at this time.
One thing which has emerged from the discussion of this present situation is that the highest hope we can have at this time is that through the combined efforts of the people who are united in the cause of freedom there may be long years of stability out of which, in God's good time, peace and an extending measure of freedom may be carried to the whole world.
No member of this house, including the members of the government, can foretell with absolute certainty what may happen a year from now, two years from now, ten years from now or 25 years from now. The most we can do is to put forth every effort we are called upon to exert to give to the cause of


freedom the strength it requires to face the threat with which it is confronted at this time. Nevertheless we do recognize that this situation may continue to exist for a long time to come. Perhaps for most of the lifetimes of all the hon. members in this parliament, we are going to be living under some form of threat to the free system to which we adhere. Surely, therefore, this is a time for us to examine with the utmost care the way in which we can best carry forward into the years ahead the fundamental principles of our free parliamentary system without in any way limiting our ability to perform effectively the share of responsibility we are called upon to accept in this great joint endeavour.
Perhaps a year from now much may have changed. I mention that because the act we have under discussion does not come to an end this year but comes to an end on the 31st July, 1956. Why then is it necessary for us to deal with this act without giving to it all the consideration that can be given? It is even possible that in the wisdom of divine Providence there may be a much greater measure of international stability a year from now. If that were so, I would hope that we would all be anxious to return as much as possible to the methods of parliamentary procedure and parliamentary responsibility which have stood the test of time under this system of ours. Our free system-that free system we are trying to preserve against all the threats which have been described in such ominous words-is a system which relies mainly upon the supremacy of parliament and the rule of law. We are a monarchical democracy. We are a member of the commonwealth. We have a federal system under our own constitution. All these things are special attributes of our own Canadian form of democracy. But the fundamental strength of the democracy rests upon the supremacy of parliament and the rule of law.
At this time I ask that all hon. members, and particularly those with legal training, consider carefully how far we can safely go in short-cuts which remove from parliament its real authority and deny, in fact if not in name, the rule of law in any substantial measure. It is not enough to say that these powers have not been enforced. If the powers that exist are powers which are contrary to these fundamental principles, then at a time when we are devoting so much of our thought, energy and treasure to the defence of that system, it surely is appropriate that we should carefully examine how we preserve these powers under the special conditions under which we live.

No matter what may have been said or what arguments may have been put forward in 1951, as we look forward to the years ahead with the hopes that grow out of our expanding strength, surely it is a time for us to examine all the facts, to examine the measures that are put before us and to find how these can be best framed to preserve the fundamental principles upon which our system rests while denying to the government no essential powers to deal with those emergencies that might arise under the pressure of events that can be readily foreseen. This is no mere legal or academic question. This building, the facilities offered to us for our meetings here, or the beauty and the dignity of these surroundings, all have no substantial importance unless the principles are effective in preserving the freedom that we proclaim.
Mr. Chairman, there is plenty of time to re-examine this measure. I would hope that the Prime Minister would seize this opportunity to carry out the statement which was made on behalf of the government in 1951 to the effect that some of the powers in this bill are special powers which should not be of a continuing nature, and to find how best the powers that are needed can be defined and described without leaving the wide, unlimited powers which have existed over these past few years. It is not enough to say that these powers have not been employed. The very fact that these powers might be used to persuade somebody to do something, without the actual formal exercise of those powers, is in itself a sufficient exercise of those powers to put us on our guard at this time.
This is not some new subject, Mr. Chairman. This is not something that we consider now for the first time. It is something that has been reviewed from time to time in the past, and those who were conscious of the conditions which were needed to maintain the vitality and the integrity of our system have always asserted the necessity for maintaining the supremacy of parliament and the rule of law. None have been more vigorous in asserting those principles than have the lawyers of this country whose training has made them aware of what it means for any person to find himself charged or to find his rights in any way denied under executive measures which have not in advance defined the rights of the individual or the penalty which might be imposed.
Sometimes it does no harm but does a great deal of good to examine ancient records in order to see the way in which the minds of people of other times were engaged with this very problem. I think there is a
Defence Production Act strangely familiar sound to these words from the "Letters of Junius" written nearly 200 years ago when he was discussing this very question of the removal from parliament of their full authority over the affairs of the people. May I quote these words:
We can never be really in danger till the forms of parliament are made use of to destroy the substance of our civil and political liberties: till parliament itself betrays its trust by contributing to establish new principles of government; and employing the very weapons committed to it by the collective body to stab the constitution.
At that time the warning was being given that under the form of parliament powers may be conferred upon the government which could stab the constitution, or which could deny the supremacy of parliament and the rule of law. It is a warning which has been repeated over and over again by those who have considered the effects of delegated powers of this nature.
Mr. Chairman, the nature of the threat of any departure from long-established practices is not to be measured by what has happened; it should be measured by what could happen at some other time. I am not attributing to any member of the government any motives other than those stated by those who have put forward their support of this measure. In these serious days we are all citizens of Canada deeply concerned about the future of Canadians growing up in this great land of ours and their freedom in the years ahead. I would not seek to draw any distinction between the sentiments of any member in this house in regard to the future of Canada, and of the people who will live in it in the years ahead. The statement has been repeated to us over and over again that this may be a long and tedious struggle for freedom, which we hope will reach a secure peace in the years ahead without the blight of such a terrible war as is now pictured to us as a possibility.
Let us break new ground. Even though four years ago it may have seemed wise in the mind of the government to go farther than some of us thought was desirable at that time, let us accept the proposition which they put forward that we are going to live under conditions of this nature for some time, and, recognizing that, to remove all powers which are not essential. This would restore to this parliament a feeling of its own authority, a feeling that it has that supremacy over the business of the people which is, in fact, the very basis of our free system.
We must not, Mr. Chairman, let this system of ours merge into something else by default. Even if we accepted without challenge the very high estimate which, from time to time, has been expressed by members

Defence Production Act opposite in regard to the almost boundless capacity of certain members of the government to meet the present and foresee the future, even if we were prepared to go as far as some of the members opposite have gone, that would not protect us from the charge that we have failed in our duty if we forget that the laws we pass are not laws for individuals. These are laws for any individual, and should not be passed at all unless they would be safe in the hands of any government that might be formed.
We have seen here and in other countries the extension of the power of government under the pressure of war and the events following two world wars. Without reviewing all the arguments we have had in the past, let us recognize the extent to which that encroachment upon our procedure has already been made, and decide that this is an excellent opportunity to review the situation and to approve a measure which will start us on a new course. Let us frame a law that does, in fact, preserve the authority of parliament and the rule of law, while giving those powers that are necessary to meet the kind of continuing threat which we see before us and which is likely to continue for some time to come.
By all means, Mr. Chairman, we must not drift by default into some form of dull and uninspiring collectivism in the name of patriotism and prompt action. It is so easy to say that there are great dangers, that we must be ready to meet those dangers. We all subscribe to the proposition that we must face the dangers and prepare ourselves for all eventualities that may come. We have all subscribed, without reservation, to the principle of joint action to defend our security, our freedom and the peace which has been bought at such a price in blood and treasure. No single word that has been said is in any way a challenge to the basic proposition put forward on behalf of the government, which I have already quoted, that in view of the kind of world in which we are now living it is essential that we have a department of defence production staffed with experienced and efficient personnel, and with the powers to perform those operations on a continuing basis. With that, we all agree. We want that done in a way that will meet all our requirements.
It would, however, be a Pyrrhic victory if, at staggering expense and tremendous national effort, we sustained our free system against all Russian threats but in doing so destroyed these very principles upon which our free system rests.
Let me repeat, even though they have been
mentioned over and over again, that those
principles are the supremacy of parliament


and the rule of law. I ask the Prime Minister to recall the words used in support of this measure in the first instance, at the time the bill which later became law was introduced in his name. I quote those words as found at page 836 of Hansard for March 2, 1951:
There is no particular significance to this date, other than to recognize that some of the powers sought in this bill are special powers which should not be of a continuing nature.
We take the word of this government, and we take the general knowledge that is available to us, that we are going to live for some time under conditions such as these. We ask the Prime Minister and the government to take this opportunity to chart a course that may conceivably be not only one of great moment to Canada but one of the turning points in the history of our parliamentary democracy.
I have no thought of going into detail as to the abuses that might occur or to quote some of the rather strong statements that have been made as to the way in which this act could be put into effect. I simply take the statements of the government itself as to the purpose of this act, as to what it means, and I point out that since the motion now before us calls for the setting up of a department of defence production with powers to carry on its activities, we subscribe to those principles. In putting forward the arguments we do, we certainly are not challenging the fundamental proposition now before us. Believing, however, that there are important issues which have themselves been so clearly stated on behalf of the government, we think that every member in this house should carefully consider the history of our system and what it means for parliament to be really prepared, what it means for our people to know from day to day the laws under which they must operate and the penalties that would be imposed if they failed to observe those laws.
Whatever exceptions there must be to those general principles under the unusual circumstances in which we live, let those exceptions be limited in clear and understandable terms, as they have been in some other jurisdictions. While our systems are not the same I would point out that, in the United States, where many of their business activities are similar to ours, their defence production act has more than 600 sections, in order to define in clear and understandable terms many of the powers conferred by that act.
I would also remind members in this committee that in the United States they have committees of the congress with wide powers to call witnesses and to demand the production of papers, which gives them a far wider measure of control in any event over special

legislation of this nature. Those who are carrying on operations of this kind very close to us have felt it advisable to define the powers in much wider terms, even though they have a broader measure of supervision than we have here.
I do strongly urge once again that between now and the time the bill comes before us the Prime Minister consider the opportunity presented to this government to give leadership in returning in as full a measure as possible to the members of this House of Commons the fundamental principles of our democratic system, the supremacy of parliament and the rule of law.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want first to say that we in this party agree with the assumption that under present world conditions it is wise, if not essential-indeed, I think it is essential-to have a Department of Defence Production which will allow us to be well prepared for any eventuality. We understand that the world now stands in a half light, a sort of dusk, half way between peace and war. We are conscious of the fact that preparedness for any eventuality is absolutely necessary if we are to prevent the shadow of the H-bomb, which now overhangs us, becoming the twilight of our very civilization.
Four years ago, when the Korean war was raging, the Prime Minister came before the house and said, in effect, "I have a brain child. I am going to introduce a bill which will set up a department of defence production on a temporary basis. This bill will also give the minister responsible for that department wide and sweeping extraordinary powers." The Prime Minister suggested that we should approve this brain child, that we should go along with her and support her. We pointed out that we did not think she was especially handsome. She had many features we did not like.
The Prime Minister was quick to admit that in any case her life span would not be very great, that in effect she was almost a monstrosity but that we could put up with her for a short time. Therefore he called upon us to be charitable and to go along with this child of his. He asked us to support her and to escort her-to take her at least as far as the Korean war. We pointed out very diplomatically that we did not like her looks, that we did not like her flat feet, her bowed legs, her under slung jaw and her horse face. As a matter of fact we said she had a face that only a mother could love. "But", we said, "under the circumstances we will be gallant and will co-operate with you. We will accompany this brain child at least as far as the Korean theatre."
Defence Production Act
The Prime Minister said that was all that was required. After all, if this girl had to go to the Korean theatre by herself, accompanied only by her relatives, she might develop an inferiority complex; and, besides that, what would the neighbours say? Under the circumstances, we in this party reluctantly went along with the suggestion. The Prime Minister said, "As soon as the show is over you can have her back here in the house, and forget about the whole thing".
What has happened? As soon as the Korean show is over-and it is barely over- and at a time when not all Canadians are out of that theatre, the Prime Minister rushes up to us with a shotgun and says, "I have the Minister of Defence Production here, and he thinks you ought to marry the girl."

"After all", he says, "besides that, if you do not, then I am afraid she will feel that her future is not very secure. It is the same thing, anyway".
Now, Mr. Chairman, it may be that a reluctant date-at-the-theatre and an until-death-do-us-part proposition may be the same thing, in the minister's language; but it is not the same in mine. I do not intend to be taken in by that kind of proposal.
The other night the Minister of Defence Production seemed to chide hon. members in this party when he said, in effect, that we supported the bill reluctantly four years ago, and that now we are talking against it. Let me point out that the proposal confronting us today and that which confronted us four years ago are not the same at all. Four years ago the bill was introduced on a temporary basis. I know the minister has told us that the proposition now is very much the same as it was four years ago. If that were so this opportunity to discuss the merits of the bill would not automatically have arisen.
When the minister was speaking about the Defence Production Act on March 2, 1951, he said, as reported at page 839 of Hansard:
By and large, these are the powers that are now contained in the Defence Supplies Act, which, hon. members will notice, is only being suspended during the life of the present proposed act. Other powers are of an extraordinary nature but fitted to the extraordinary circumstances of today.
Because the cold war of that time had become a shooting war, we in this party went along with the proposal then made. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra stated our position at that time in these words:
Mr. Speaker, because of the very serious situation which Canada is facing at the present time, and because of the ever present threat of war, members of the official opposition have no intention of

Defence Production Act opposing this particular resolution or the bill which will follow it, unless that bill turns out to be in terms which are objectionable.
The then member for Nanaimo, now the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, also very ably expressed the position of our party on that occasion when he said this at page 873 of Hansard of March 2, 1951:
In this respect, that I agree in principle with the setting up of this Department of Defence Production. I realize, as he does, that the minister in charge of the department must be given certain powers in order that teeth may be put into the legislation so as to enable him to produce the equipment so essential for our defence forces. Like him, I feel there should be no unnecessary powers, or powers which are not essential, given to the minister. That point has been dealt with, and I shall not refer to it again.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, it is abundantly clear that four years ago we went along with this temporary act because we were in a hot war at that time and extraordinary steps had to be taken because of the extraordinary position in which we found ourselves. I repeat, we realize at this time that a Department of Defence Production on a permanent basis is essential, but we do not agree that the wide powers that are given the minister under the present act should be made permanent. After all, we should not put ourselves in the rather ridiculous position of forfeiting the freedom which we are setting out to defend in the process of preparing to defend it.
Most of us in this group are veterans of at least one war, and therefore we cannot be accused of being unsympathetic to the point of view of the military men. We know the tragedies of going into battle ill-equipped with obsolete arms, and we do not want that to happen again if we can prevent it. Nevertheless, we will not abandon the position which we are sworn to defend just to make the stockpiling of arms a little more convenient. The Minister of Defence Production might say that that sounds very pleasant but it is academic, we must display horse sense in these difficult times. I say that for me horse sense is not good enough. I know the sense of horses fairly well. I know that horses will not approach voluntarily any real or apprehended danger; I know they will not approach it without a struggle. But I do know that you can turn a horse around and back him into a fire, into deep water or over a precipice and he will not object. I am .afraid, Mr. Chairman, the Russians know our horse sense too well. There is more than one way of winning a cold war. The Russians recognize that if they can back us into a position they want us in, it will be just as successful as a frontal attack. I would regret seeing any Canadian government taking any action which even remotely smacked of panic.


After all, in a cold war we cannot solve all our difficulties by using exclusively the methods which won for us in the last war. It is not open warfare to begin with. It is too easy a solution to say that the government can take extraordinary powers and stockpile a great amount of munitions, or even the latest and most efficient types of armaments. The problems of the age of the H-bomb are more difficult than that.
We are in a cold war which is a permanent condition. We must be able not only to defend ourselves if the cold war flares up into a hot war here or there, but we must also have long-range planning which will make open warfare unattractive to our enemy. That includes efficient civil defence and a long-term planning for the dispersal of our vital industries so that three-quarters of our industries and about one-fifth of our population will not be wiped out overnight by a few H-bombs.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I have related my remarks to the resolution in my own mind, and when I have completed my remarks I think you will see, Mr. Chairman, the sense of what I have to say.
The bill suggested by this resolution is not, in my opinion, the answer to our present problem. As I have already said, the cold war is a permanent proposition. It is apt to extend into the future as far as any of us can see, and therefore we must be prepared to take our part in it under conditions which will be permanently acceptable. The provisions of the present act are not acceptable if they are put on a permanent basis.
The proposed bill to extend the life of the present act has for its purpose the winning of the cold war and the prevention of a hot war. Our purpose is to attempt to preserve our civilization as we know it. If we acquiesce in any way in the giving up of our freedom we shall create pleasure in the minds of the men of the Kremlin because they know that it is very easy for people under this type of program to go on beyond the point of no return. It is not the policy of the men in the Kremlin to win control of the world by an all-out war.
I believe that the policy of the Kremlin is to win world control through the demoralization of the peoples of the free world, to bring about a chaotic state of affairs in which communism can easily take over control. That

has been the pattern so far and I have no reason to believe that it will change. The Russians are following that pattern for a very good reason, and that is because they know their history. History teaches us that great civilizations of the past, almost without exception, fell, not because they were conquered and overrun by external powers, but because they crumbled from within.
I say in all sincerity that at this time the Prime Minister perhaps more than any other person in Canada is the custodian of the freedoms which we have inherited. It behooves us all to see that our freedoms are handed on unimpaired to posterity. I think therefore that in this cold war which will go on as long as we can see we should enact legislation only which will be acceptable on a permanent basis. After all, dreadful as it seems, we must accept cold war conditions as being normal conditions, for the rest of our lives at least.
I have a suggestion to make which is in line with the similar one already made by the Leader of the Opposition. I suggest that a bill be introduced which would set up a permanent Department of Defence Production along much the same lines as any other department of government. That bill would of course repeal the present Defence Production Act, and repealing the present Defence Production Act would automatically end the suspension of the Defence Supplies Act which was passed in 1950. I think that this house would accept very readily the setting up of a Department of Defence Production if the act was limited to the physical setting up of that department and if the powers which were to be granted to the Minister of Defence Production were outlined by the Defence Supplies Act amended as considered suitable. In that way we would avoid this confusion of having both propositions in the same bundle.
The powers which might be granted from time to time to the Minister of Defence Production could be adopted on their merits as occasion required without implying in any way that the Department of Defence Production should not be carried on on a permanent basis. I think that a happier solution could be found to the problem now confronting us if the Prime Minister would see fit to reconsider the position.

Third, he may accept the interpretation, in which event the act stands exposed in all its authoritarian nakedness and the fears of the hon. members for Eglinton, Greenwood and Vancouver-Quadra, as well as those expressed by my leader this afternoon, stand completely justified. Mr. Pallet!: Mr. Chairman, I could not let this occasion pass without making some comments on this resolution. I would be shirking my duty as a member of this house if I did not rise and say in the strongest terms possible that the resolution extending the powers of this act to no definite date is one of the greatest setbacks in the history of democracy in this country which I have seen during my short term in parliament.
This house at one time begat a monster and that monster begat another head. As a result of public opinion the first head was chopped off; that was the Emergency Powers Act. It was felt that the second head, the powers under the Defence Production Act, would die a natural death in 1956. Consequently, attention was not drawn to it. The people of Canada were not aroused concerning its dangers and on a quiet winter day in 1955 we see a resolution, short in length but mighty in effect, which purports to extend the life of the department with all its insidious powers.
I would like to draw a comparison. Let us assume for a moment that the minister who administers this act is the minister in charge of national defence. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, an exact comparison of the powers he seeks under this act would have full-out conscription for the army under the Department of National Defence. He is asking for powers to deal with industry and the manpower involved in industry, powers which we would not have given to the Minister of National Defence to deal with the actual manpower of the country. Just think of that comparison for a minute, Mr. Chairman. It is a complete denial of the free enterprise system which this government claims to espouse. The government takes great credit for the production of Canada when it can say, "We point to it as a free enterprise system." While pointing to it with one hand as free enterprise they simultaneously point with the other hand and say, "This is not


free enterprise, we are not clever enough to enter into contracts with you which would cause you to perform the things we want you to perform. We have this club and if you are not good boys we will use it."
As the Leader of the Opposition has said, the fundamental principles for which many Canadians have laid down their lives, and for which a great portion of the national budget is allocated, are being laid on the altar under this act.
After all, a man working at a machine in a factory in this country has certain rights. This resolution suggests the rights of the man working in a factory can be taken away by the minister. What does it mean when a minister can say that a manufacturer is not performing his duties properly and the minister is taking over his factory? It simply means the minister is taking over the workmen in the factory and is taking away the individual rights of the people in the plant.
The action is much deeper than would appear by this resolution. The hon. Leader of the Opposition said that in 1951 his party took the word of the government that this act was of a temporary nature. By the introduction of this new resolution one can see how much the word of this government is worth. The question is self-answered.
I have often wondered, and I ask myself today, how many of the members who sit behind the minister who administers the department which this resolution concerns know exactly the terms that are contained in the act? The hon. member for Eglinton outlined some of the terms very carefully. They go to the very depths and roots of our system. They take away, on the strength of one man's opinion only, whoever the minister may be who is in charge of the department at the time, every right to which we have pledged ourselves in the past and to which we expect others in the future to pledge themselves.
I suggest, as have other hon. members before me, that a resolution could easily have been introduced which would continue the life of the department but at the same time give it only the powers necessary for carrying out its work under our system of freedom of the individual and of enterprise.

We do not wish to be niggling about the particular definition of powers. We do wish, however, to see some effective limitation imposed on the powers in this bill, which now are sweeping and untrammelled in their nature.
In this measure the government is proposing to take away the one effective limitation. I do not say it was adequate, but at least it was an effective limitation. It was one in point of time. Nothing is offered to the house by way of a substitute to control these powers. The minister will have everything hereafter that he has at the present time or has had since 1951, even in the face of a greatly changed world situation.
I have another question, Mr. Chairman, and that is about the power of the minister under section 27 to appoint a controller where he is satisfied that someone has failed to enter into a defence contract or is likely not to perform in a businesslike and efficient manner a contract into which he has entered. Has any situation arisen yet where the minister has found it necessary to exercise the powers conferred upon him by section 27 to appoint a controller?

That situation arises where we have set up a plant for a particular job. I shall use this as an illustration, but not to indicate that action has been taken or is likely to be taken at this plant. Take the Orenda engine plant in Toronto; we

Defence Production Act built the building and installed the machinery. I think the building cost $17 million and the machinery about $40 million. We sold the building back to private industry, and under the arrangement the government will continue to own the machinery. It will be used for the purpose indicated. Suppose we saw that through bad management the plant was failing to produce what was required? In other words, that as a result of bad management it was not turning out Orenda engines to what we believed to be the capacity of the plant. Suppose we find the plant going bankrupt as a result of bad management? We had similar cases in the second world war, a number of them.
Are we to stand by and see the efficiency of the plant drop or see the plant go bankrupt, and face the inevitable consequences of either event? No; we reserve the right, if the owners will not change the management or if those responsible will not change the management, to insist that the management be changed.

We in this group are not reluctant to point out the anti-social characteristics sometimes displayed by private industry. But I suggest, Mr. Chairman, none of us has ever made any stronger indictment of private industry than that made this afternoon by the Minister of Defence Production. If he, as an ardent defender of the private enterprise system, feels that in the face of national need legislation of this kind is necessary, I suggest that point should be considered even by my friends to the right who are also strong protagonists of the private enterprise system.
I need not spell out or repeat the instances the minister cited this afternoon. The statements he made were very serious, and I suggest that they do indicate the need for parliament to establish certain economic controls and to put those controls in the hands of the government, when you have a program of defence procurement and defence purchasing on a scale such as we have at the present time.
I listened with a great deal of interest to the speeches made by my hon. friends to the right, such as the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra, the Leader of the Opposition, and the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, particularly as they submitted in strong terms the need for the rule of law. I take second place to no one in my interest in the rule of law. I shall remind my friends to the right of that phrase on some occasion that will arise not very far in the future. Nevertheless, I do not intend to be fooled by those who would equate the rule of law to the unfettered right of private industry to be a law unto itself, even in the face of national need.
I am ready to admit that this act should be thoroughly studied by all of us before we agree to the bill at the second reading stage. I hope that between now and then the government might consider whether some changes in the act itself might be made. I suggest, as one change, that instead of wiping out the expiry date altogether another expiry

Even as I have asked my hon. friends of the Conservative party to pay attention to what the Minister of Defence Production has said in asking for this legislation, so I would ask the government to pay attention to the suggestions put forward from this side, including what has been said by members of the official opposition.
Meantime, as I see it, a case has been made for the continuance of economic controls to protect the economy against the effects of defence purchasing, defence procurement and defence building, and on that basis it seems to me this resolution should be allowed to pass.

I say it is on the basis of arguments which are directly related to the principle of this resolution, and which we would want to analyse from all points of view, that we have to reach a decision.
I want to say that I have reached my decision, and it is that if the minister or the government who have had to deal with problems in Canada at a time of national emergency have in their experience found it necessary to have certain powers in order to get the co-operation of private business in Canada, and if the government and the minister who are still in power feel that the Canadian and world situation is still such that in the national interest they require to have this authority in case it is required to get co-operation under this system, then I am going to support a minister with experience, a minister who supports private enterprise and who says, "I need these powers in the event of a national emergency in Canada". speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to say just a word or two before the resolution is passed or voted upon, whichever may be the case. I have listened to the debate on this resolution for the past few days. Back in 1951 when the Defence Production Act was brought before this house I made it clear on behalf of the group I represent that we realized the need for placing in the hands of the minister those wide powers required to meet the situation and to protect the Canadian economy. We did not feel that it was any reflection on private enterprise. It was a situation which had to be met and which required wide powers in the hands of

the government for regulatory purposes, wide powers which industry itself in the country was asking for for its own protection.
We did think at that time that the government was wise in placing a time limit of five years on the act, but we felt also that it would be perfectly justified in having the act terminate say on July 31, 1956. It has now been indicated by the minister that as we draw somewhat closer to the terminal date he feels it is going to be necessary to repeal section 41 of the act, which indicates to me, at any rate, that he thinks it will be necessary to make the terms of the act permanent.
I do not like it. I believe that even though it may be considered essential to grant a continuation of the powers under the act it would be wise for the government to consider placing a terminal date in the bill. I agree with what was said by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in that regard. I would not like to lend my support to the repeal of section 41. Before bringing down the bill I believe the government should consider including some terminal date, if not the one suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, of July 31, 1958, at least something that is reasonable.
If the government will do that it will have my support for the continuance of the act. I support the resolution, but certainly if the government indicates that there is to be no terminal date at all, that they are going to make this act a permanent act, I would have to consider my position most carefully before I agreed to a continuation of the act.

Perhaps I might explain the difficulty. If it were not for the human element in the department I would be quite willing to set another date and debate the matter again. However, the difficulty is that the Department of Defence Production is staffed by civil servants. The dollar a year men have gone; they served their time, and we now have trained civil servants occupying the positions. Over 1,000 men in the department are to all intents and purposes temporaries. In other words they are in a department that is due to expire on a certain date.
The reason I had to announce that the government would undertake to make this a permanent department was that the men were leaving me because I could not promise them a position for more than a year. We have very able men in the department who should not have been placed in that position. They were men who could have taken excellent positions in industry. They could do better in industry than they could in the
Defence Production Act government. Their attitude was that they would stay if they could be guaranteed a good future in the government, but if this was not the case they would go elsewhere, where they could be certain that their services would have a future.
That is the reason for asking that the time limit on the department be removed, which action in effect changes the department from a temporary department to a permanent one.

I gather from what the minister said that the only reason for leaving the duration of the act indefinite was to assure the people employed in the department that their jobs would be continuing.
That suggestion gives me the greatest alarm, because certainly those men will want to maintain an act which will give them a job for probably 20 or 30 years. If we are legislating for their welfare I think there is a far safer way of doing it. I would far rather propose that we guarantee them jobs somewhere else during that 20 or 25 years than to undertake to guarantee it to them by a bill of this kind which, as the hon. member for Peace River points out, certainly means the establishment of dictatorship and can be in no way interpreted otherwise.
What conceivable chance has the opposition of obtaining a review of this act once it is passed and goes into the records? What assurance have we that ten years from today there will be in charge a man who will be as sane, as wise and as responsible as the present Minister of Trade and Commerce? I do not hesitate for a minute to say that I think what the Minister of Trade and Commerce has done, with the tremendous powers he has had during the last few years, has been admirable. I do not see how a man could have done any better. But let me say this. We do not often find a man like the Minister of Trade and Commerce; we do not find more than one in about every million. We therefore must take precautions to see that the country shall be reasonably safe no matter what kind of minister gets into that position.
I certainly would not be in favour of letting the resolution pass. It must be recognized, Mr. Chairman, so that those reading Hansard will understand it as we in this house understand it, that the only chance in the world we have of holding up this act is right here at the resolution stage. The government can ride roughshod over us at any other stage, but it cannot ride roughshod over us at this stage. If we propose to hold up the resolution we can do it until next Christmas or longer. This is where the opposition has some chance of asserting the right of the people against a government that may be disposed to use too much power unwisely. speechtext: Is the minister going to make any statement or explanation with regard to the meaning of this resolution?

maintopic: ASKING OF QUESTIONS ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT AND DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman. I have a short statement which I hope will be helpful. The bill which will be introduced in consequence of the adoption of this resolution will be entitled "The Canadian Forces Act, 1955". It will be similar in title and scope to the Canadian Forces Act enacted by parliament in each of the past five years,

from 1950 to 1954. In fact it is a more or less routine bill designed to make a number of what we consider desirable amendments to statutes affecting the armed services. This year the bill is more limited in scope than usual, in that it contains proposed amendments to only two acts, namely the National Defence Act and the Defence Services Pension Act.
Thirteen clauses of the bill contain proposed amendments to the National Defence Act. These amendments deal with a variety of subjects and would effect a number of changes in military law and procedure. Several of them are designed to give added protection to accused persons. Others it is hoped will facilitate the administration of justice under the code of service discipline.
One of the most important of the proposed amendments would repeal the section of the National Defence Act under which members of the forces are given wide exemptions from judicial process, and would substitute therefor a section exempting only the property used by members of the forces for military purposes from execution under civil judgment.
Another proposed amendment would permit an officer or man who has been released from the Canadian forces or transferred from one component to another to be reinstated, with his consent and subject to regulations made by the governor in council, without the necessity of a break in his service where it appears equitable that this should be done.
Other amendments proposed to the National Defence Act would authorize the minister to substitute for a finding of guilty made by a court martial, a finding of guilty on an included or cognate offence-

maintopic: ASKING OF QUESTIONS ON ORDERS OF THE DAY

speechtext:
-on an included or cognate offence-that is a lesser offence-and would authorize him to order a new trial where an irregularity in law has occurred at a court martial, and would enable the judge advocate at a court martial to decide questions of law arising during the trial rather than, as at present, merely advising the court thereon.
Other proposed amendments would place certain limitations on the period during which a person may be held in service custody awaiting trial; would clarify the provisions respecting automatic remission of punishment after suspension, and would permit the return to Canada for trial by a civil court of a person subject to the code of service discipline who has committed outside of Canada a criminal offence punishable by the laws of Canada.

There are other proposed amendments to the code of service discipline that are of a technical nature and can best be explained in detail when hon. members have the bill before them.
Twelve clauses of the bill contain proposed amendments to the Defence Services Pension Act. These also relate to a wide variety of subjects. Two of the more important amendments would incorporate in that act provisions similar to those now contained in the Public Service Superannuation Act. One of these would empower the treasury board to grant a widow's pension in certain cases to women who would not otherwise be entitled thereto. The other would enable a contributor who fails to elect to count prior service for pension purposes within one year of becoming a contributor, as is now required by the act, to elect at any time whilst he is still a contributor, subject however to such penalty as may be provided by the regulation.
Another proposed amendment would authorize the governor in council to extend the provisions for augmentation of pensions upon re-enrolment in the forces or appointment to the public service, to pensioners re-enrolled or appointed subsequent to the 30th day of June, 1950.
Other amendments proposed will permit the adoption of administrative procedures designed to facilitate and expedite the payment of benefits under the act, and effect other technical changes in the act.
The foregoing amendments, Mr. Chairman, are of considerable importance to the efficient and equitable administration of our defence forces, and I therefore commend this resolution to the favourable consideration of the committee.

It would seem that they are intended to give additional protection to the servicemen, and if that is the principle of the bill then I think we could concur in it. However, we shall have to reserve our judgment on the various detailed clauses because, from the information which has been given us, it is impossible to really make a full assessment of their value. Each of these 50433-127
Canadian Forces Act
clauses will deserve careful consideration. Reference has been made to a reduction in exemption from judicial process which will apply to all servicemen. I feel we shall have to examine that clause carefully to see that the servicemen are duly protected.
Another thing that strikes me is that the position of the judge advocate general is now to be somewhat altered. In the past the judge advocate general has attended courts-martial in an advisory capacity, either he or his representative. Now he is going to be there more in an executive position, in that he will give rulings on points of law. I feel we would like to look into the implications of that more fully.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN ANNUAL APPROPRIATION TO GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Yes. On January 14, 1953, my predecessor tabled in this house a copy of order in council P.C. 1953-52 of that date by which the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada was directed to make an investigation and report on all phases of the problem of railway-highway crossings. In doing so he called attention to the fact that the number of accidents occurring at these crossings had become a matter of mounting national concern.
The board, in compliance with this order in council, carried out a very comprehensive investigation that involved the holding of public hearings at many points in Canada and the examination of a large number of submissions. On June 21, 1954, my predecessor tabled the report made to the government by the board upon completion of its investigation.
In its report the board of transport commissioners made the following recommendations:
1.	That instead of the present contribution of $1 million to the railway grade crossing fund there should be each year an appropriation of $5 million subject to the proviso that where on April 1 in any year there is an uncommitted balance of more than $2 million in the fund the appropriation for that year should be such sum as with the uncommitted balance would amount to $7 million.

2.	That the present contribution of 40 per cent of the cost of the actual construction work for the protection, safety and convenience of the public to a maximum of $150,000 in respect of any one crossing at rail level be increased to 60 per cent and $300,000 respectively.
3.	That the fund should be made available to aid reconstruction and improvement of grade separations in existence at crossings when the proposed legislation comes into force which, because of their location, design or size are inadequate for the highway traffic using them, the contribution in any one case not to exceed 30 per cent of the cost of reconstruction nor the sum of $150,000.
4.	That contributions should be permitted toward the annual cost of maintenance and operation of automatic signals installed at crossings after the proposed legislation comes into force, the contribution in respect of any one crossing not to exceed for any year the actual cost for that year nor the sum of $200.
5.	That the provision in subsection 1 of section 265 which prevents a contribution from the fund in respect of crossings at rail level constructed after April 1, 1909, unless there is the agreement referred to in the subsection between the railway company and a municipal or other corporation or person, should be eliminated but there should be a provision that the board shall not apply any money out of the fund towards the cost of work in respect of a crossing unless the crossing has been in existence for at least three years prior to the making of the board's order to apply the money.
6.	That the board should be empowered to make contributions toward the cost of highway projects which involve the construction of a grade separation and the closing of an existing crossing or the diversion from the existing crossing of nearly all the highway traffic using it.
7.	That section 263 of the Railway Act which places on the railway company unless and except as otherwise provided by an agreement approved by the board all cost of protection, safety and convenience of the public in respect of any crossing of the highway where the railway is constructed after May, 1909, be repealed.
If the present resolution is carried it is proposed to introduce a bill to make the necessary amendments to the Railway Act to give effect to these recommendations, with the exception of that providing for contributions toward the annual cost of maintenance and operation of automatic signals installed at crossings after the proposed legislation 50433-127i
Railway Act
comes into force. In other words, Mr. Chairman, the legislation is designed to give effect to all the recommendations of the board of transport commissioners save that respecting contributions to the annual cost of the signals, to which I referred a moment ago.
