subsubtopic: INCREASE IN ANNUAL APPROPRIATION TO GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, last year when the estimates having to do with the railway grade crossing fund were before the committee I made some observations on grade level crossing conditions in the municipalities of Toronto and Scarborough, and mentioned their great concern about the heavy toll of fatal accidents and the evident slow progress in eliminating the many hazards.
The Minister of Transport at that time on a point of order contended that as the whole problem of railway-highway crossings in Canada was under review by the board of transport commissioners, a quasi-judicial body, the discussion was sub judice. He found out later, however, that the board had finished its investigation and had filed its report, and subsequently apologized to the house for not having had knowledge of the fact sooner.
I now have had the advantage of having read the report on the board's studies and findings, and make the following observations on this complex problem. The board's report is replete with necessary information and will be of great value for future reference.
The commissioners held 17 public meetings and one final and general hearing. They commenced their examination possessed of an awareness of the public's apprehension that the problem was not receiving satisfactory attention. They have endeavoured to bring it into proper perspective, collating the many elements of national concern into a pattern they hope will speedily effect a remedy, but it is without a plan as to when and where to apply.
There is ample evidence throughout the report that all were anxious that the annual toll of death and injury should end. It was

Railway Act
also apparent from the start that the incidence of accident did not create or develop a policy of accident prevention, but that accident occurrences must be in sufficient numbers before elimination of grade level crossings would be considered, let alone undertaken.
Grade level crossing accidents engaged attention early in the century. The rapid growth of the railways became such a problem that the Railway Act was revised in 1888 to give the railway committee wide powers to meet the situation. In the next 20 years our railways had expanded to 20,000 miles of track with 14,000 level crossings, and in the year 1904 there were 52 killed and 232 injured, or one killed every week and one injured every other day. Notwithstanding the wider power given to the committee their efforts to abate the dangers did not satisfy the public demand for adequate and greater protection.
The government then created a new authority, the board of railway commissioners, with extended power and authority, who likewise found that the problem of grade level crossings did not lend itself to easy solution, as the crossing hazards increased faster than protective devices could be installed or grade separations built, because the resources of the railways and the municipal corporations were too meagre to keep pace with expansion, making it difficult for the new board to measure up to its responsibility of assuring standards of safeguards.
This situation brought into being the railway grade crossing fund in 1909, that provided for set sums to be voted annually for a stated number of years, spelling out the percentage to be paid from the fund at 20 per cent and the limit of cost of each project to $5,000, and only three to any municipality a year.
The board invited the provinces to contribute to the fund, adding that they would observe any condition the provinces stipulated, but the provinces declined although they did assist through the avenue of grants in aid to the municipalities.
Reporting on their first year of administering the fund, the board drew attention to the financial burden placed upon railways and municipalities.
Following this through the years and up to the present time were a sequence of amendments at set intervals increasing the per annum grants from the original amount of $5,000 to the present $1,000,000, raising the percentage of the fund's assistance from 20 to 40 per cent and limiting the cost to $150,000 a project, allowing only six projects

a year to any municipality, with the total cost of a project to be allocated on a division of 40 per cent by the fund, 30 per cent by the municipality and 30 per cent by the railways.
During this period special assistance was given from the unemployment and farm relief funds to the railway crossing fund, and special votes by parliament of $7,300,000 were made to relieve unemployment in the years 1930 to 1939. However, in the war years 1940 to 1946 no grants were made to the fund by parliament and it was during the war years that the situation got beyond us.
The total expenditure from 1909 to 1953 for highway crossing protection was $51,731,255, of which the municipalities paid the largest share, $19,250,000 or 37$ per cent; the railways paid $18,250,000 or 35$ per cent, and the railway fund paid $14,250,000 or 27$ per cent.
According to table No. 9 of the report, 1951 is the last year for which the number of level crossings is given, 32,612-although I believe it stands at over 33,000 to date-of which 3,296 are protected and 29,316 unprotected, compared with the record of 1921, 30 years ago, when there were 2,279 protected crossings and 25,699 unprotected.
It is obvious that we are slipping fast. The board itself despairs when it confirms this by saying:
This does little to encourage the hope that in the near future the problem can be substantially reduced or disposed of.
However, it does make an effort to show some improvement was made, but the figures are there to show that there was no progress.
The investigators found that the consensus of contention was that the unprotected crossings must go; that rural and urban crossings were critically inadequate in protective standards under present-day traffic; that the continuing increase in shocking accident fatalities made imperative a standard of safety rules for trains and highway vehicles at all rail crossings in conjunction with automatic signals and a planned system of advance warning signals and floodlighting of crossings, reflector signs and devices on railway cars to cope with new hazards of high speed, heavy traffic and poor visibility. They also recommended that the provinces and municipalities must recognize their responsibilities by making effective regulations and laws with increased instead of diminished enforcement.
It is also revealed that there is a tendency on the part of those paying the cost to minimize the accident occurrence and the death toll by the use of percentage figures. However, with every shocking fatal accident

Railway Act
the public clamour and insist that something must be done, and that is the real genesis of this report.
The problem of paying for these projects is one which engages the ingenuity of the board, for all through the report, repeated again and again, is their concern about the ability and capacity of the participating parties, the railways and the municipalities, to meet their obligations of the shared cost of projects. To give an idea of what the average costs in the various undertakings are:
For flashing lights and bells	$	6,100.00Annual maintenance	$	560.00
For automatic short-arm gates and
signals	$14,200.00
Annual maintenance	$	865.00
Grade separations or crossing elimination with traffic volume, soil and drainage conditions, highway and rail approaches, expropriations and property damage, produce the heaviest financial burdens, and the most difficult to bear. The average cost for them is estimated at:
Lower cost subway ranging from $78,000 to $350,000.
Higher cost subway from $400,000 to $2,100,000.
Overhead bridges from $40,000 to $725,000.
Highway diversions from $1,000 to $220,000. The general breakdown for an average urban project is $800,000, and for the average rural project $100,000. As the grade separation projects are linked up with traffic congestion and bottlenecks in urban areas, the necessity for their removal becomes urgent. The board when compiling its many tables gave the number of crossings, but failed to catalogue the grade separations or register the schedule of immediate requirements for Canada, so we must gauge the magnitude of the program by the submissions to the board by the provinces and municipalities.
Edmonton: five separations in the next five years at a cost of $6,500,000, with an additional seven required in the near future.
London: 11 railway street crossing bottlenecks estimated at a cost of $9 million.
Toronto: 38 level crossings at an estimated cost of $60 million.
Quebec: a complete railway relocation is required to eliminate the many level crossings, the cost of which has not yet been determined.
The province of New Brunswick: five hazards needing separations, plus Moncton with 13 level crossings.
The province of Nova Scotia: a large number of general grade separations, plus Halifax with the Fairview bottleneck and many main line hazards.
Prince Edward Island: 257 grade level crossings, four of which are rated as grade separations.
The municipality of Scarborough, to which I drew the attention of the house last year, requires eight grade separations and has 26 crossings which need immediate protection, and 22 which require realignment, bank reduction and sight clearance. Every province and 45 municipalities, which included all the larger cities, were listed as presenting claims.
The report clearly sets out that the problem, in the board's opinion, is not wholly a safety and accident prevention problem, as the great majority of grade separations are determined on other grounds such as population growth, urban development, and the tempo of life that places a high value on motor vehicle services, demanding a free flow of highway traffic through eliminating stops, delays and congestions at grade crossings.
While the answer to the grade crossing problem is grade separation, the board points out it must be realized that when costs are high, and the capacity and ability of any of the participating parties to pay is feeble, or if they are unwilling to pay, then the less costly crossing protection will have to suffice. Benefits from a grade separation are measured and compared with the costs so that, when built, it will give the greatest return.
Certain broad general conditions must prevail to warrant the costly grade separation instead of the less costly protection, such as increased value to the economy, enhancement of residential and industrial values, improved business, greater parking facilities, greater street capacities with unimpeded fire and police services, and a general tone of welfare to the community.
In applying the data obtained in their survey the board have been able to give a picture of the cost of an all-embracing program of grade crossing elimination and grade crossing protection. They estimate, for the whole of Canada, a total cost of between $655 and $700 million; and, if spread over a period of 20 years, the annual cost would be $33 million. But they qualify their conclusion by saying that at the end of the 20-year period only 1,433 grade level crossing hazards, or less than 5 per cent of the total number, would have been eliminated.
They again pose the question of the participating principals' ability to support any or all of their share of the actual costs the benefits would impose on them; and that other projects not in the category of grade level railway crossings would have to be neglected or abandoned. The board dismisses

Railway Act
the proposition of embarking on a wholesale program that would, in a few years, speedily and permanently dispose of the grade level railway crossing problem as outside the realm of possibility, and submits the following reasons:
1.	That the cost, $655 to $700 million in a hypothetical selected program, would complete less than 10 per cent of grade level projects in Canada.
2.	That the benefits would not warrant the enormous cost, and grade level railway crossing accidents were less than 1 per cent of all highway traffic accidents; and other useful necessary projects might rank in priority.
3.	That the federal government could not support the entire program, and it would strain the resources of the railways, municipalities, and most of the provinces; and the money might be spent in areas where least needed.
4.	That a heavy demand would be made on the engineering and technical staffs of the railways, provinces, and municipalities, and would limit the work attempted.
5.	That it would interfere with the removal and relocation of railway lines and highways.
If time permitted I would show the fallacy and weakness of the contentions in their five reasons. However, I shall make no comment on the first three of these reasons, other than that you will come to the same conclusion I arrived at: that the board was seeking escape routes to avoid facing up to and resolving the real issue.
The fourth reason will confirm my conclusions on the first three when they state:
That a heavy demand would be made on the engineering and technical staffs of the railways, provinces and municipalities, and would limit the amount of work attempted.
The colleges turn out year after year from their classrooms the calibre of men and women we need for this work. We lose a great number of the young men and women who have graduated from our colleges in emigration to the United States and other countries year after year because we have no place to employ their skill and talent. We cannot say the amount of work attempted would be cramped because of lack of staff. This work is the very thing we are constantly searching for. It offers employment to our young men and women who have graduated from our colleges, and they are earnestly seeking for such opportunities. You can see the kind of thinking the board has given to this phase of the problem.
The board did not give much attention to, nor did it elaborate upon the future increase

of population by natural growth and immigration, and the industrial and commercial expansion and the impact it would have on the problem, through the increased volume of highway and railway traffic in the years ahead.
The board again emphasizes the fact that it is far beyond the municipalities' and railways' ability to carry the burden with their financial resources. Well, from our knowledge of the municipalities' plight we have to go along with them in their contention that the general inflation, in vogue through the government's inability to hold it in check, has added to their difficulties. This is also reflected in the high cost of education, public works and social and welfare services, and is further aggravated by the federal and provincial governments' taxes which take so much of the people's income that even a moderate increase in municipal taxes is impossible, because the general level of the people's wages and income has not kept up with the faster pace of inflation.
Provincial governments help the municipalities to the extent they feel is warranted by the various projects, and to the extent that their financial resources will permit; but no definite policy has been established, and if it were not for this assistance the municipalities could not have undertaken some of their major projects.
A major part of the report is occupied with analyses, some factual and some conjectural, with checks, benefits, values, responsibilities, allocations, limitations, approaches, and examinations; but it always trails into the avenue of the participating parties' ability to pay, so that it becomes an obsession with them, to the extent that they have obscured the main terms of reference of their commission, namely:
(a)	conduct a survey and report on the methods considered by the board to be practicable, under all pertinent circumstances, of eliminating hazards and improving the public convenience and the protection and safety of the public at such crossings;
(b)	review and report on the adequacy of the railway crossing fund to provide for construction of works for the protection, safety and convenience of the public at such crossings;
(c)	make such recommendations as the board may deem advisable in the premises.
Why do we have this report, and the bill that now proposes a revision and amendment of the present act? We have them because of the incessant demand from every community in the Dominion of Canada where there is a railway crossing hazard for an increase in the appropriation by parliament to the railway grade crossing fund, adequate to put an end to the expanding catalogue of gruesome and fearful accidents. As each accident occurs, and the press relates the

shocking details, fresh impetus is added to the pressure by the public that something be done to put an end to it.
I have pointed out, and often, the board's continued reference to the municipalities' and railways' inability to pay. I have done so because I want to emphasize their penchant for strolling from the main intent of the terms of reference, namely to eliminate hazards, and improve the public convenience and the protection and safety of the public at such crossings.
While the report is important, and a valuable source of information, it has only confirmed what the public already knew, namely that enough is not being done to stop the nation's mounting toll of railway grade crossing accidents because enough funds were not being appropriated to the railway grade crossing fund; that the problem has long since got away from them, with the race about lost; and that they are not now going to be satisfied with this new piece of stop-gap drop in the bucket legislation, because it only mirrors again what has happened in the past.
Do the board or the government think the public are going to be deceived with the report's double talk, when they state on page 53 that while within the limitation of fixed funds on the one hand, and the increasing costs of protection on the other, it may be concluded that protection has kept pace with the crossing problem, and their use of percentage figures in table No. 9 in order to establish their conclusions? The factual figures show there were 1,128 protected urban crossings in 1921 and that 30 years later, in 1951, there were 1,597, or an increase of 469. That is good; yet there were 2,873 unprotected urban crossings in 1921 and 3,883 in 1951, an increase of 1,010 unprotected crossings, a fact which tells an altogether different story.
The same pattern is repeated in the rural areas. Disregarding the protected rural crossings, which showed an increase of 548, the unprotected urban and rural crossings showed a total increase of 3,617 in the same 30 years ending in 1951. That is an alarming increase that cannot be explained away by percentage figures. This increase certainly refutes their contention of keeping pace with the problem.
I have previously mentioned that they have applied to accidents this technique by which they arrive at an accident frequency in the years 1946 to 1952-when there were 604 accidents at 1,771 protected crossings-of 4-9 per year per 100 crossings, and when there were 2,455 accidents at 29,316 unprotected crossings for a frequency of 1-2 per year per 100 unprotected crossings. The public are
Railway Act
not fooled, either, with this percentage juggling. They know averages better, and they grasp these gruesome facts for the same period of 1946 to 1952 in this way. There were 3,059 accidents, or an average of over one a day; 980 were killed, or someone was killed every two and a half days; that 3,404 were injured, or over one a day-some permanently disabled-at a level crossing somewhere in Canada.
The public cannot be deluded. They are not interested in the percentage of people killed or injured in relation to so many miles of railway or to so many thousand motor vehicles per mile of highway. They want to know, and that soon, how and when these accidents are to end; and that is what the terms of reference specified.
This problem from the start has been scantily dealt with, with never enough to tackle the job properly and a narrowness in scope; and even now the board's recommendation, which appears generous when compared with the present appropriation, is a continuance of the same old policy of too little and too late. The board has failed by not coming to grips with this great works project, having compiled tables and charts on everything but the one thing that is most essential, namely the number of grade separations, the number of short-arm gates and signals, the number of bells and automatic signals, the number of railway and highway diversions and relocations needed; in fact, a complete listing of every project that is deemed necessary by the municipalities, provinces and railways, and the estimated cost thereof. If this information were available, the House of Commons would then realize how gigantic this problem is, and that it goes far beyond any previous idea we have held. It is a project so huge that it dwarfs the St. Lawrence seaway project, inasmuch as it stretches from coast to coast.
Using the board's hypothetical selective program-and their assumptions were based on past experience-as an example, the board set the cost at $655 million, and they said this amount would complete only 1,433 projects or about 5 per cent of the existing 29,316 unprotected railway grade level crossings. The committee will readily sense that the real cost would be in the $5 billion bracket, that it is now beyond the board's capacity to handle, and that their recommendation of $5 million a year, compared with their estimated cost of $33 million a year for a period of 20 years, would accomplish only 5 per cent of the work to be done. They will realize that this is only toying with the problem, and how futile and hopeless the amount of $5 million would be with the

Railway Act
object of overcoming the railway grade crossing menace which the people are demanding should be overcome and to which the terms of reference refer.
Let us consider the yearly average of construction, namely 10 grade separations and 90 protected grade crossings that $1 million a year is now producing. If this average is multiplied by five, the rate of progress would then be stepped up to 50 separations and 500 protected crossings a year. You will realize how slow we shall be moving and how ineffectual the sum of $5 million a year will be, even with the advantage of the board's increased share in the cost from 40 per cent to 60 per cent, and the reduction of the municipalities' share from 30 per cent to 25 per cent and the reduction in the railways' share from 30 per cent to 15 per cent; you will observe that we are arriving nowhere.
This dilemma we are now in, through our grade level crossing problem, can be used to develop a plan to relieve our unemployment situation which the committee now knows is recurring each year and is prevailing now. That is a plan that can fit into and be integrated with other scheduled public works projects, because of the great flexibility that grade crossing projects allow; you can start them where and when the unemployment is most acute. Unlike the St. Lawrence seaway project they are not confined to one area. The broad mantle of this huge railway grade level crossing project is comprised of thousands of work projects of various sizes and descriptions, and one could be picked out to fit the need in any particular area. With modern techniques in use today in outdoor construction, such projects could be started any time of the year, a consideration which unfortunately does not apply to road building.
It is evident that we shall have to support the resolution before the committee which implements the board's recommendations, and be thankful for this small mercy in the nature of a few crumbs that fall from the government's table to relieve the anxiety of our people who are imploring that this slaughter at our railroad crossings shall be stopped by elimination of the hazards that cause it.
I believe this is a fair summation of the board's report which, to me, reveals 25 years of frustrated effort. I believe the government should realize that this railway grade level crossing problem is out of control, and that it is their duty to augment further the funds now recommended so as to tie the project in with their other works projects and relate it to our unemployment problem. Then it will be the solution of the railway grade level
fMr. Small.]
crossing problem and will relieve the unemployment situation, if the government will incorporate it into a well planned, long-term schedule by creating jobs when the employable unemployment tension is most acute and at its peak.
I expect that I shall be regarded as impertinent for giving this resume of the board's report and making a rough synopsis of it. If I have made it appear that the board are inured to their position by being continually importuned from every section of the dominion for more to be done than their limited funds will permit, I want it to be on record that they are held in high esteem and are regarded as martyrs to a cause, trying to perform a hopeless task that a parsimonious government has imposed upon them.
The debates on unemployment and war veterans allowances should have made it clear to the government that where the suffering of our citizens is concerned-whether through the tragedies of want or tortured agonies at our railway crossings-the people of Canada do not want shabby treatment to be accorded in the alleviation of their distress, and are willing to share the cost.
It is now too late to make any immediate relief works effective to remedy the present unemployment, owing to the government's inertia. However, the railway grade crossing projects can be put on the Prime Minister's desk for placement at the top of the agenda for discussion at the forthcoming dominion-provincial conference to be held in April. At that time plans could be made to cope with the problem of next year's seasonal employable unemployed, in order to avoid a repetition of the government's nonperformance during the winter of 1954-55.

maintopic: ASKING OF QUESTIONS ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN ANNUAL APPROPRIATION TO GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
In introducing this resolution, Mr. Chairman, the minister indicated that the proposed legislation will implement the recommendations of the board of transport commissioners, with one exception, namely that provision be made for the maintenance of automatic signal devices, which the board suggested should be set at not more than $200 per year.
In considering the proposed legislation, one must do so in the light of the problem with which it seeks to deal. The main recommendation would appear to be increasing from $1 million to $5 million the annual appropriation for the railway grade crossing fund. There are also to be changes in the administration of that fund, namely in the amount which the fund will pay, which is to be increased from 40 per cent to 60 per cent of the cost of any one project, and the amount that can be granted to one project will be raised to $300,000.

The board of transport commissioners have presented a very good report dealing with the railway grade crossing problem in Canada. I am not going to deal with the report because the previous speaker put a great part of it on the record. I do feel, however, that the background material in the report gives us some idea of the growing magnitude of the problem.
The minister spoke of this problem as being one of mounting national concern. I think it is interesting to note that in 1909, when this fund was set up, automobile registrations in Canada totalled some 5,000. Since that time the number of automobiles in Canada has increased by 640 times, and I believe the total registrations are now in excess of 3,200,000. When we consider this trend, together with the increased cost of providing crossing protection, we can understand the magnitude of the problem which this legislation proposes to meet. The board has mentioned several instances where certain projects would cost in the neighbourhood of $2 million or more.
As the minister pointed out the board, in its recommendations, suggested the contribution to the fund be increased from $1 million to $5 million. Of course, that is only part of the picture. If you read the report you will find that the board of transport commissioners suggested a program which they felt would be necessary to meet the problem today. The cost of this program would be in the neighbourhood of $655 million. The board has suggested that if this were spread over a 20-year period it would amount to an annual expenditure of $33 million. When we consider these recommendations, we begin to see the amount of money set aside by this legislation in its proper perspective. As the previous speaker has pointed out, even this ambitious program suggested by the board would not cover more than between 5 and 10 per cent of the crossings in Canada. I want to stress the fact that while the board made a specific recommendation concerning the $5 million, they did point out that any worth-while effort would involve an expenditure of $33 million per year.
Under those circumstances, and taking into consideration the fact that in Canada less than 10 per cent of our railway crossings are protected while in the United States around 16 per cent of the railway crossings are protected, I think the figure proposed in this legislation is very inadequate indeed. Of course all members in the house will welcome the increase in the contribution from $1 million to $5 million, though I feel that many of us will have grave misgivings as to the adequacy of this increase.
Railway Act
In its public hearings across Canada the board of transport commissioners heard representations from many municipalities and other highway authorities. The board suggested that almost all parties appearing before the board at public hearings stated there would have to be a substantial increase in appropriations to the fund. Where the parties making submissions made reference to particular figures, the recommendations ranged from $4 million up to $30 million. It is quite evident, therefore, that in the opinion not only of the board of transport commissioners but also of all other parties in Canada who are interested in this problem, the increase in the appropriation would have to be much higher than is called for in this legislation.
I should like to point out now that the mere appropriation of a sum of money does not necessarily mean that that money is going to be used to do the job. In introducing the resolution the minister pointed out that any money left in the fund, when added to the annual appropriation, could not exceed $7 million. This clearly indicates that the government is satisfied all the money is not going to be used up each year. There is going to be a considerable amount of that money left over at the end of the year. They have, therefore, set a limitation of $7 million on the amount of money that can be carried over for this purpose.
I feel that the reason for suggesting the money might not always be used up is quite obvious. The grants in aid principle is not an altogether sound principle. It is all very well when the other parties to the agreement are in a financial position to take advantage of any appropriations which may be made available. If we find that money is available in the grade crossing fund and municipalities are unable to make the contribution required by the terms of the act, then that money is not going to be used and the job is not going to be done.
I suggest that a rigid formula, such as is contained in this legislation, is going to mean that a great many municipalities in Canada will not be in a position to get work done that is absolutely necessary. We must point out that the legislation calls for an increase from 40 per cent to 60 per cent in the amount that may be spent out of the fund. So far as that goes, it is quite satisfactory. It will ease the situation to some extent. But as a matter of fact it is questionable as to how many municipalities at the present time are going to be in a position to take advantage of grants made to this fund. I think this problem was evident at the very time the fund was set up. As a matter of fact, if hon. members will refer

Railway Act
to page 25 of the report they will find that the commissioners have quoted from the report of the board of railway commissioners in 1909-10. I shall read a sentence from that report, which says:
The expense of a separation of grade is always a costly work. The local municipality almost always objects to contributing, and of course should not contribute as much as the railway company; in some instances it should not contribute at all.
So within one year of the setting up of this fund it was agreed by the board of railway commissioners that there are instances when a municipality should not be called upon to contribute anything toward a project. And it seems, Mr. Chairman, that if that condition obtained in 1910, then the municipalities are much less able to play their part today.
There is little question that over the past 40 years municipalities and provincial governments have been called upon to provide additional services and to assume financial burdens which were not envisaged 40 years ago. So the municipalities are less able to contribute to any great extent to this work at the present time than they were at the time the fund was set up. I suggest the commissioners at that time felt there were instances in which municipalities should not be called upon to pay anything toward projects, and that situation certainly obtains in this country today.
If the most effective job is going to be done under this legislation, then grants from the fund will have to be made in a more flexible manner than is outlined in this legislation, and I believe that under certain circumstances the administrators of the fund should be empowered to pay up to 100 per cent of the cost. There is no use having a formula that is going to deny to the municipalities the chance to correct this great national problem as it is found in their localities. I think the way to get around the situation, as I have said, is to empower the board of transport commissioners to use discretionary powers to grant, under circumstances based upon priorities, in accordance with the greatest need, and having regard to the element of danger at grade level crossings. The board should be empowered to pay out of the fund up to 100 per cent of the cost.
There is one other extremely important aspect of this problem. Thus far I have been discussing the question of the railway grade crossing fund from the standpoint of protection and to some extent the convenience of the travelling public. But the other aspect I would like to mention this evening has to do with our present unemployment situation

in Canada. No one can deny that at the present time Canada is faced with a very serious unemployment problem. For many years we in this group attempted to get the government to face up to the realities of the economic situation in the years immediately following the war, and to plan to maintain full employment in Canada. We have urged, in the years when unemployment figures have been mounting, that the government should take the necessary measures to provide employment for Canadians.
At the conclusion of the second world war many Canadians were led to believe that the government had this matter in hand. We heard much talk about a shelf of public works. The suggestion was made that when unemployment developed the government would reach up on the shelf and take down public works projects to provide employment. A few years later we found that this was merely a delusion, that no such shelf of public works had been set aside by the government.
So the situation today is that, in spite of the fact that over half a million men and women in Canada are unemployed, the government has no plan whatsoever for the alleviation of this distress. The only piece of legislation which could be tied in any way to the problem of unemployment was the recent legislation dealing with the unemployment insurance fund, and I do suggest that improvements in unemployment insurance legislation do not provide employment.
Under the circumstances I suggest that we must look at this problem not only from the standpoint of protection but also from that of providing at least a measure of employment opportunity for Canadians in various parts of Canada. There seems little doubt that this work is the type that can be fitted into measures to relieve unemployment. As the previous speaker pointed out, many of the projects have already been considered and planned by municipal governments. I am sure there are many municipalities throughout Canada that have had plans for the building of subways and other grade separation projects, that have been gathering dust on the shelves for many years.
It is quite clear that projects of this kind could be put into operation within a reasonable length of time. Then again, this is a problem which is not concentrated in one particular part of Canada; it is found from coast to coast. Therefore any measures of this type can be used in those parts of Canada where unemployment actually exists, and it is quite general throughout the country today.

With this in mind I wish to suggest that what I have said is not new. Anyone who wishes to refer to the report of the board of transport commissioners dated May 10, 1954, will find at page 27 a section dealing with special appropriations for grade crossings. The report goes on to point out that-
Apart from the statutory appropriations to the fund, there have been two other types of financial assistance made by the federal government for this work.
In the first instance sums of money were transferred to the unemployment relief fund in the early thirties. As a matter of fact, in 1930 the sum of $500,000 was transferred direct from the unemployment relief fund to the railway grade crossing fund, to be used in accordance with the provisions of the act. Other appropriations were made purely as measures to relieve unemployment. That is to say, the ordinary statutory provisions regarding the spending of that money did not apply in those cases. There were direct grants of money, without such strings attached as one would find in connection with sums of money under the legislation.
As I said, in connection with the first type, in the year 1930 half a million dollars was turned over to the railway grade crossing fund, and in 1932 another $500,000 was transferred. Parliament approved a special vote of $500,000 in 1934. There was a special vote of $300,000 in 1938, and a vote of $500,000 in 1939.
Those sums of money were added to the statutory grant, at that time $200,000 per year, to the railway grade crossing fund. In addition there were sums of money paid out by the government for highway crossing protective works, by way of unemployment relief funds. These grants were not restricted by the statutory provisions governing the fund, and there were certain differences between the types of grants made.
The board sums it up in this way. In the first instance, the board authorized payments out of these special funds, subject to the approval of the governor in council. Second, they could be applied to existing subways and overhead bridges as well as level crossings. Third-and this is very important-contributions could be made to the cost of the projects up to 100 per cent. Fourth, in orders making grants from such funds there were to be special provisions in regard to the working hours of persons employed on the works for which the grants were made.
At that time the general rule had been 70 per cent; the fund would pay 70 per cent of the cost of projects. However, in many cases the full 100 per cent was paid. The 50433-1281
Railway Act
board relates that sums of money were appropriated in each of the years from 1935 right up to 1939-40, $1 million in each year, although I notice in 1937-38 some $1,064,000 was appropriated. Therefore we had three types of appropriations. First of all there was the statutory appropriation under the legislation, which at that time was $200,000. In addition we had money transferred from other government sources to the railway grade crossing fund, which had to be spent in accordance with the provisions of the act. Then, third, there were contributions made directly as a public works project to alleviate unemployment distress at that time.
If the government had followed this principle in other fields during the 1930's, Mr. Chairman, a great many of the millions of dollars that were poured down the drain, spent on direct relief with nothing to show for it, would not have been spent in that way. We would have had something to show for all the vast sums of money that went into direct relief during the time of the last depression.
In view of the record, apparently there were no difficulties at that time in transferring appropriate sums of money. I suggest we could adopt the same principle here. I suggest that we accept the proposition that we need an increase in this fund from $1 million to $5 million primarily as a protective measure, and incidentally a measure which would be necessary if there were no unemployment in this country at all. This measure should have nothing to do with that.
Of course any government expenditure will have some effect on the unemployment picture, but primarily the legislation before us now can be viewed on its merits as a measure to provide greater safety at our highway crossings in Canada, but I suggest and rather suspect that the government looks upon this measure as something to be used in the alleviation of the unemployment problem in Canada. I rather believe the government feels that this legislation will do more than provide a measure of protection. If that is so, then the government should extend this principle and make satisfactory contributions to the fund.
I have not dealt with the technical aspects of grade crossings because the problem is well understood by all hon. members. I do not think there is an hon. member in this house but has personal knowledge of a great many rail crossings in his own constituency which pose a great threat to traffic. I know in my own constituency there are a great many dangerous crossings, some of which might be

Railway Act
protected by automatic signal devices, but a number can be protected only by subways or other grade separation projects. I think that is self-evident.
The problem is there. The board of transport commissioners went into it extensively and outlined the problem we face today; but I do feel that we have to view this legislation from this point of view. I am sure we accept the increase from $1 million to $5 million, although we have reservations as to the adequacy of that amount. Indeed, the evidence seems to suggest that that amount is wholly inadequate. In view of the fact that recommendations have been made by interested parties to the board of transport commissioners, and at every opportunity they advocated substantial increases in this fund; taking into consideration the fact that the board of transport commissioners themselves indicated the need for an extensive program in this country, which they outlined as costing around $655 million, I feel that hon. members cannot do other than look upon the amount provided for in this legislation as inadequate.
In view of the serious unemployment situation in Canada I believe that if the government would take a leaf out of the history book of a few years ago, and in addition to the statutory grant of $5 million would make additional sums of money available in terms of the ratio between the statutory grants and the sums of money which were actually expended during the 1930's-and remember a dollar went a lot farther in those days than it does today-they could well afford to add to the $5 million mentioned in this legislation an additional amount. I know it will not be done through this legislation; but if this job is to be done, then the government ought to bring in supplementary provisions to add to this fund an amount of money with particular reference to the unemployment problem in Canada at the present time.
The government could well afford to appropriate the sum of $15 million in addition to the statutory grant of $5 million; for one thing is certain. This problem is one which will have to be met. Every time we pick up a newspaper we read of a tragic accident. I noticed in the Gazette this morning a picture which I am sure a great many hon. members saw. It was a picture of a car which had been sliced in two in a crossing accident in the city of Montreal yesterday. One can hardly pick up a newspaper without noticing the loss of human life and property damage which has occurred at unprotected crossings. I will admit that in many instances the human element enters into it, errors of human

judgment. Nevertheless, it is up to us to do as much as we can to eliminate these accidents.
With respect to the unemployment situation, which is most important at this time, I ask the government to make provision for supplementary legislation of some type to make available to this crossing fund a sufficient sum of money to make not only a frontal attack on the great level crossing problem in this country with respect to safety, but also to make some small contribution at least toward the alleviation of unemployment in Canada.

Wherever it was necessary to cross the main line the provincial government saw to it that overpasses were put in. It is quite true that they are expensive and run to large amounts of money, but I do not think we should be too much concerned with the cost. I recognize immediately the minister's difficulty in raising sufficient money to carry on an enterprise of this kind, but if we can save one life by putting in an overhead crossing it seems to me the money would be well spent.
When the minister is making his plans for this project I think he would be well advised to bring in the provincial ministers who are responsible for this type of construction and see what co-operation he can get in moulding an over-all plan for crossing construction so that we will be able to eliminate, I was going to say 90 per cent but certainly as great a number of these crossings as is humanly possible. It has been suggested that this could be considered as a relief project, but in my opinion it should not be. I take the same view in this connection. I am not underestimating the importance of providing public works for assistance to the unemployed,
Railway Act
but this should not be considered as an enterprise of that kind. It should be undertaken as a project which is essential, and which I am sure every Canadian will welcome in that it will provide protection against the loss of life. The sooner this plan can get under way the better it is going to be.
As I said a moment ago, I think it would be quite useless for me to dwell longer on what the government should and what they should not do. When the bill comes down we will know exactly what they are going to do. I hope the minister will see to it that the legislation to be brought down will be sufficient to meet the requirements; that there will be the closest co-operation between federal and provincial authorities, and last but not least that he will not permit financial considerations to be placed in the way of constructing these most necessary projects. Money should not be the main consideration. Due consideration should be given to the protection of life, which all Canadians are desirous of bringing about at this time.

speechtext:
Contrary to the opinion expressed by the hon. member for Bow River, who said money should be no object, I think I might say money definitely is an object in connection with this debate.
The hon. member for Danforth and the hon. member for Regina City both referred to the serious situation in connection with the financing of this project by the various municipalities. It seems to be a common habit here to answer any requests by having someone on the government benches stand up and tell us how many millions of dollars the government is already spending for this type of improvement. The critical point concerning this project is the difficulty of the municipalities in providing the necessary finances.
I think this difficulty arises from two main causes. First there is the limited tax base which is available to the municipality and second, the proximity of the municipality to its tax base. The municipality feels very quickly any changes in economic conditions and trends. The chief burden the municipality must bear now arises from the fact that large masses of additional people are moving into most of the urban centres, causing an immediate requirement for services of all types. Probably education is the chief and

most immediate service they must provide. These services must be provided before the municipality has an opportunity of laying its hands on the tax revenues the newcomers may produce.
That problem does not confront us here. As a matter of fact, when additional people arrive in the various municipalities there is an immediate prospect of funds becoming available to the federal treasury from income tax and sales tax on the items purchased by the new arrivals.
The situation confronting us is certainly not brought about by the home owner, who has to pay a fairly substantial portion of the cost of grade separation. I said in connection with the unemployment debate that houses were not out of work, people were. I say tonight that houses are not going to go through the grade separations, people are.
This problem has arisen because of the terrific increase in the number of motor vehicles presently owned by every section of our population. I might say they are therefore the people who should pay for this type of construction, but I am certain their first answer would be that they are already paying. I am certain they feel they are paying fully for any type of amenity they receive in connection with road construction and grade separation. In advancing that argument I might refer to the Public Accounts of Canada, 1954, volume I, which contains some material which is enlightening so far as motorists are concerned.
The federal government collected $94,715,040 from excise taxes on automobiles. On the sale of rubber tires, tubes and items of that kind it collected $11,381,716. I can only estimate the amount of sales tax it collected, and I base my estimation on the brief of the Canadian Automobile Association which was presented to the Minister of Finance on September 10. It would appear that sales taxes provided the federal treasury with approximately $90 million. In addition we must consider the taxes on the importation of automobiles of all kinds and I am sure this could probably be worked out in round figures amounting to $25 to $50 million. This does not take into account the millions of dollars which are collected from the people of this country and are included in the corporation taxes paid by the car manufacturers in Canada. I think I can leave it to you to conclude that the figure we are talking about is in the area of hundreds of millions of dollars.
What does this government do for the motorist? I have searched far and wide, and I find it is recorded in the same book that the government spent approximately $13,378,998 on the trans-Canada highway last year.

Approximately another $400,000 was spent in administering this fund, survey services, etc., and approximately $1 million was spent on services. In addition to this I assume we should charge in an item for the parkway system in Ottawa, which totalled approximately $750,000. I am sure the federal government collected between $225 and $250 million last year, but apparently it is only prepared to spend approximately $15 million on motorists.
If we were living back in the horse and buggy days, or if we were only concerned with pedestrians, there would be no requirement at all for this type of construction. There appears to be no doubt the people who use this type of construction are already paying 100 cents on the dollar for it, and it should be provided for them. In that way and in that way only are we going to be able to remove from the municipalities the burden which is being placed upon them in the proportion they must contribute to this construction.
How much will we accomplish? I read an article which appeared in the Weston Times and Guide of Thursday, March 10, 1955, to the effect that a subway or underpass is planned for construction at the corner of Royal York road and Dundas street west in my constituency. I understand there has been agitation for this since 1917. Perhaps with this magnificent increase in the federal government's fund it is possible that it will eventually be constructed. However, a few days later, on March 14, 1955, I read an editorial in the Globe and Mail to the effect it has been necessary to remove from the metropolitan Toronto budget some $6,500,000 for capital construction in this municipality and two others. We see therefore that the problem of financing these projects is upsetting the budgets of the municipalities. The editorial also pointed out that Toronto proper has had to cut its budget by $10 million.
I made a point of contacting the reeve of the municipality in this constituency, and he informed me this particular construction which has been asked for since 1917 was knocked off the books even before it got this far. As to the danger which has been spoken about by other hon. members, and the critical financial situation the municipalities are in, it seems to me that the only way in which these difficulties can be overcome is by a realistic approach to the whole tax problem. I am quite sure we shall not get that approach until we have the dominion-provincial conference, which has been asked for by almost all the parties in this house.

Mr. Chairman, coming as I do from the railway centre of Nova Scotia, I feel that I should say a word of commendation to the minister and the government for introducing this resolution. I am looking forward, as a result of this legislation, to at least the elimination of some level crossings in our province.
As was said by the hon. member for Halifax a few moments ago, there are almost 1,000 level crossings in Nova Scotia. Some of them are protected by signals, but most of them are without any protection whatever. I understand, of course, that this fund will be administered under a four-way program among the provincial government, the municipalities, the railways and the board of transport commissioners. I would assume that in the first few years, possibly quite a large proportion of the money would be used in connection with the trans-Canada highway. That is all to the good.
Nevertheless, many of the accidents which have taken place on our highways-and there have been far too many of them-at level crossings have not been on the main roads. They have not been on the main railway lines. They have been on branch lines, or lines of railway with only three or four trains a day running over them. Many accidents at level crossings take place on such lines. It was only a couple of years ago when, in my own constituency, six or seven people were wiped out on a short line on which there were just two trains a day. Those people got in the way of one of them and the whole family was wiped out.
I was going to express my hope that a considerable amount of this money will be used in erecting signals on roads other than our main roads. The elimination of level crossings on the main roads in most cases will merely tend to speed up traffic; and as so frequently happens, when you speed up traffic in one place people merely get into greater trouble elsewhere. It might be a greater lifesaver if some of these signals were put on our secondary roads. The old slogan that any time is train time is certainly true today. One thing that I believe could be done to great advantage would be to erect far more signs at railway crossings just bringing to the notice of our people this slogan: "Any time is train time".

speechtext:
I believe all members of the committee will be glad to vote for this resolution. The fact of the matter is that many of us would like to vote for it four or five times. In other words we feel that the steps being taken are good and in the right direction, but that they do not go far enough.
The Minister of Transport and others on the government side no doubt feel that they are quite virtuous, in that they are implementing most of the recommendations made by the board of transport commissioners in connection with this matter. As a matter of fact the minister has pointed out that the bill will implement all but one of those recommendations. Even before this stage of the legislation is over I hope he will explain why it was decided not to implement that one particular recommendation, which had to do with a contribution toward the annual cost of the maintenance and operation of automatic signals installed at crossings after the recommendation came into force.
With regard to the request that has been made particularly from the opposition side of the house, namely that more should be done than was recommended in the report, I should like to read a couple of sentences from an editorial on this matter which appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail of June 29, 1954, shortly after the report of the board of transport commissioners was tabled in the House of Commons. These are the sentences I have in mind:
The board is to be congratulated for making these long-needed changes in the terms. But in doing so the commissioners only underlined the magnitude of the problem they refused to face realistically when they turned their attention to finding the dollars necessary to solve it.
I share that view, namely that the board are to be congratulated for the recommendations they have made, but I suggest that in their report they have but underlined the magnitude of the problems. They should have recommended sufficient dollars to meet it, and so I am interested in this concluding comment in the editorial to which I have referred:
If the board had set the figure too high, it would have been parliament's duty, when the recommendations are converted to legislation-in time, we hope, for the next session-to cut it down. It should be, therefore, parliament's duty to find the courage the board lacked and increase the government's contribution to the fund to the point where it will be possible to protect all dangerous crossings.
I think many of us in this committee share that view, namely that there was a failure on the part of the board to envision what is really needed in this country in terms of protecting the dangerous crossings.

Like others who have spoken, I come from a part of the country where we are in sore need of a number of grade crossing separations. As I pointed out in the house last year, there is one in particular for which I have been asking over a number of years. Even while we have been making these requests on the floor of the house we have had further accidents and further loss of life, particularly where the main lines of the railways come into and go out of our city of Winnipeg.
There is just one other comment I want to make, Mr. Chairman, because the ground has been well covered by my colleague the hon. member for Regina City and others who have spoken in this debate. I should like to urge the Minister of Transport and others in the government to become even more interested-more involved, if you want to put it that way-in this whole question of the loss of life on our highways, both at level crossings and in other ways.
As hon. members on the other side of the chamber will know, last session some of us tried to persuade the Minister of Justice and others on the government side to take the lead in calling a conference on highway safety, in order to see whether something could not be done to cut down the loss of life on our highways both at railway crossings and in other ways.
I was disappointed when sessional paper No. 179-A, which was tabled on Monday, February 21, 1955, in response to certain questions of mine, indicated that no one in the federal government had given consideration to inviting the appropriate representatives of the various provinces to meet for the purpose of discussing the matter to which I have now been referring, despite the fact that this matter was discussed in the House of Commons on April 1,1954. Amongst the ministers who indicated that no consideration had been given to this matter was the Minister of Transport. However, Mr. Chairman, this is one of the main reasons I wanted to say a few words just now, and 1 shall be very brief.
I was pleased to note that the Canadian Good Roads Association has taken the lead in calling a conference to be held at Ottawa May 24th to 26th, which will be under the distinguished patronage of the Governor General, and which will be chaired by a gentleman most of us in this house know very well, the Hon. Brooke Claxton. I understand that this conference is to be attended by many representatives of provincial governments and many representatives of other organizations in this country, in an effort to see if something can be done to increase the safety element upon our highways and cut down the loss of life.

As you may have sensed already, Mr. Chairman, 1 am going a little bit afield, but not far. I admit I am talking about something that goes a little beyond the loss of life occasioned by automobiles colliding with trains at railway crossings, but I suggest it is related. I hope the Minister of Transport, because of his concern with this legislation, will go further and see that his department or the government is also represented at this conference to be called by the Canadian Good Roads Association, I am sure that anything anybody can do, including this government, to try to cut down the loss of life in these ways will have the support of every member in this house, that where ten years ago we ment will see that it is represented at this conference. Let us do everything we can to achieve greater safety at our level crossings and on our highways generally.

maintopic: ASKING OF QUESTIONS ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN ANNUAL APPROPRIATION TO GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Probably every member in this house has at some time witnessed a grade crossing accident, has seen the wreckage or met the victims, or perhaps has had a very narrow escape from such an accident. I feel that grade crossings are a major problem in this country. I believe our program is far behind that of most of those countries in which I have travelled. You will not find one unguarded level crossing in most countries in Europe.
Unemployment is the most pressing problem we have at this time. If we are indulging in any public works to create employment, this is the most useful work we can do. I must say that I feel an amount of $5 million is altogether out of line with the needs of this country. At a limit of $300,000 for each job, such an amount would allow only 16 jobs to be completed in Canada. My city of Kitchener alone could use a good part of the $5 million to correct the many dangerous crossings at which many people have been killed.
The idea that gates protect people is not correct in all cases. I personally had an unpleasant experience in driving onto the railway track at our principal crossing in Kitchener, namely the King street crossing. I found the gate on the far side lowered before me when a train was approaching. I started to back off the track and found the gate closed behind me. Luckily it was a wide crossing or I would have been obliged to crash the gate. The same thing happened at this same crossing to at least one other person of whom I know.
The city of Kitchener has a problem at the King street crossing, where traffic is blocked regularly and queues of waiting cars are formed stretching for blocks. When fire
Railway Act
trucks or ambulances are blocked at this crossing it could be very serious. 1 urge that the $5 million should be increased to at least double or perhaps triple that amount for this year or other years when there is unemployment. Unemployment is serious in my district, as is the problem of level crossings.

maintopic: ASKING OF QUESTIONS ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN ANNUAL APPROPRIATION TO GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
From what has been said by various hon. members tonight, Mr. Chairman, one can only conclude that this is a very pressing and very grave problem so far as danger is concerned. While the $5 million mentioned here is a very small amount, it is a gesture in the right direction. All the hon. gentlemen tonight have talked more or less from the standpoint of money, and being a woman I am going to talk for just a few minutes from the standpoint of the preservation of human life and property.
I should like to speak particularly in connection with what we call secondary roads, to which one hon. member referred, or what hon. members who come from the rural areas will know as township or county roads. These roads present very grave problems, particularly here in the province of Ontario. What is true of the province of Ontario, Mr. Chairman, is true throughout this country, around and near the great centres. We find that population, in great numbers and heavy concentration, is now moving out into our rural areas. I think my county is a fair example of what is happening in this nation, if 1 may be pardoned for using it as an example.
Even three years ago a large part of my county of Halton was a rural area, but there is now a heavy concentration of population and industry which is growing every day, every week and every month of the year. For example, in that county we have 19 concession or what we call township roads running north and south. We have as many roads running east and west, which the farmer members will know we call side roads.
Across these 19 concession roads run three of the main lines of the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific railways. We have the line running from Toronto right through to Buffalo and New York. Then we have a double track line running through the central part of the county from Toronto through to Detroit. At the northerly end of the county we have another double track line running from Toronto right through to London and Sarnia. Bisecting the county from north to south we have the Hamilton railway line that runs into the northern part of Ontario.
That means, Mr. Chairman, that there are at least 75 level crossings in the county, in addition to those on the Queen Elizabeth

Railway Act
highway, the Dundas highway, No. 7 highway and No. 5 highway. These are all crossings that are virtually unprotected, and for the most part they are relatively in the same condition today as they were years ago, in spite of the increased traffic.
I can say very conservatively, and I am sure I will be supported by other members in this house, that where ten years ago we had one car passing over a given crossing, today we have 100. They are going to the Ford plant and to other industries too numerous to name. There are school buses. Today we have consolidated schools, and the children are going in these buses across these dangerous railway crosssings. The plants are on 24-hour shifts. The men are going along the highway hurrying to get to work, and they are hurrying back home at night. Then there are the women going back and forth to various kinds of business. You can see, therefore, that this is a very real and very serious problem. Every day it is a matter of potential death and damage to property.
As one goes through the county you see that the road signs leading to these main railway crossings are in the same condition they were many years ago. They have not been modernized. One of the reasons for that is that these townships or municipalities look after these signs that warn of the approach to these main railway lines. These are heavily travelled roads. I would say that one of the things that should be considered and as to which experiments should be conducted is the standardization of a method of protecting the railway crossings across this country.
In this way the people in my county of Halton, as well as others in counties right across the country, would be familiar with standardized methods of protection. In addition to that, there should be some centralized authority such as the railway board or some such body, which would accept the responsibility for placing the protective signs and looking after the roadway approaches.
As recently as last Friday evening I passed over one of those crossings in my county, in which a double-track high speed line is involved. As I approached I noticed that the crossing was hidden by a great amount of shrubbery and trees growing along the right of way. This growth had not been properly cleaned out. The sign that was there was old, and apparently had been there for many years. There was no way of seeing it readily, because on it there were no reflectors, or if there were any they were practically invisible at night.
In my view a standardization of protective measures, under a proper authority, would
'Miss Bennett.]
not be expensive. There is no necessity to spend hundred of thousands of dollars. In discussing this subject we do not need to talk in millions. I believe we could have an adequate protection of human life and property if the standardization were centralized under a proper authority that would be responsible all across the country. We should look into this matter, and experiment with the proper types of approach. We must decide whether the approach would be best with a curve, or if it should be straight, or whether there should be an incline. In other words, what procedure should be adopted to effect the greatest preservation of human life.
Then we could have new types of signs. None of these things would cost very much. Such signs could carry adequate reflectors so people could see them at night. While I cannot give the figures for the whole of Canada, I believe it would be safe to say that at night there are more accidents from cars running into freight trains than from freight trains running into cars. It has been stated in the report-and this suggestion should be considered-that reflecting material should be placed on freight cars passing over railway crossings so that people who are approaching such crossings would be able to see them. Then, as we find already in some provinces, consideration should be given to setting the rate of speed, such rate to be observed throughout the country.
I have no desire to detain the committee, but I would repeat that if adequate protection were given many hundreds of accidents could be prevented. I repeat that we would do well to standardize our methods right across the country, and that there should be a centralized authority dealing with these methods with a view to seeing that they are used properly and adequately throughout the country.

maintopic: ASKING OF QUESTIONS ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN ANNUAL APPROPRIATION TO GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to associate myself with those who have complimented the minister upon placing this resolution before us at this time. I do not do so because of any belief that it will solve the problem of unemployment, because I do not think an expenditure of $5 million on level crossings will solve that problem. However, it is certainly an indication that at long last the government has come to realize that something must be done about level crossings. While this may be only a beginning, it is a recognition of that vital problem.
May I compliment the lady member who has just taken her seat upon bringing to the attention of the committee the fact that there are hazards in addition to those offered by level crossings. She has mentioned the presence of trees and shrubbery; and when

she did so I was reminded of a crossing on the Westminster highway leading across Lulu island where the trees and white guard railings are just in line with the line of vision of the automobile driver, thus frequently obstructing his view and making it practically impossible to see what is coming down the track.
It would not cost very much to eliminate these obstructions and reduce the hazard which is found in similar situations in all parts of the country. The fact that the expenditures in war years interfered with the amount of work done on level crossing projects has culminated today in the greatest rash of level crossing accidents in the history of our nation. Coupled with that is the fact that there are more automobiles on the roads than ever before, travelling at higher speeds and with greater horsepower. In many instances drivers are forced to place reliance upon signals that do not exist. We find that in many instances, through mechanical failure of signals or for some other reason, accidents occur.
The hon. member for Regina City has suggested that this expenditure might serve to relieve the unemployment situation. I do not believe so, because this $5 million is only a drop in the bucket. As I suggested earlier, I believe this expenditure should be made for humanitarian rather than for other reasons. It is true that the improvement of grade crossings would require the employment of a certain number of people, but I am convinced that $5 million spent in the building of houses, or something of that nature, would do more to create jobs for those requiring work.
Now to get back to the level crossing problem, I have in mind the summer resort community of White Rock in my constituency in which, normally, some 6,000 or 7,000 people live. But on some Sundays one can find as many as 30,000 people at the beach at that point. Anyone who is familiar with White Rock and the surrounding area will know that there is only one possible way of getting to the beach, and that is by crossing a railway track which is situated about 100 yards from the beach. There is no underpass or overpass, although the area would lend itself very well to an improvement of that kind. The location of the track would render it a comparatively simple matter to put in either an underpass or an overpass.
As I said earlier, there is no possible way of reaching that beach except by crossing "the railway track. In the time I have been there I have known of at least one death at that point, a year ago when a small child was killed. We know that children crossing
Railway Act
the track do not watch with as great care as adults, with the result that they are injured.
It seems to me the main purpose behind this legislation is to provide means to eliminate hazards of that kind. If I felt for one moment that the resolution was offered only as a means to help solve the unemployment situation I would not be too enthusiastic about it. I look forward to the minister examining the problems in areas where one would expect to find a heavy influx of people across railway tracks. He would have to decide whether it would be possible in such instances to create a pedestrian crossing or one suitable for motorcars.
The other matter I should like to deal with is this. Where we have new railway lines built or in the course of construction, such as the Pacific Great Eastern in British Columbia, I would strongly suggest to the minister that the Department of Transport bring in legislation to make it possible at a nominal cost to have roads travel over or beneath the railroad itself. There are thousands of such places in the mountains of British Columbia, and I am actually amazed every time I take a tour through the province to discover how few overhead passes or underpasses we have in British Columbia. In many places it would be a simple matter to change the road a very little bit at a relatively small cost and thereby save hundreds of thousands of dollars or the millions of dollars that we are talking of spending at this time.
I would suggest that before approval is given to the actual route of the trans-Canada highway, these points be kept in mind. It is most important to save money, but we can still do a good job in this country by thinking of the safety of life and at the same time saving for the taxpayer some of his hard-earned cash.

maintopic: ASKING OF QUESTIONS ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN ANNUAL APPROPRIATION TO GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wish to take a moment of the committee's time to support the suggestions put forward by the hon. member for Halton. I believe that in many parts of the United States there are approach signs to level crossings which read "Stop, Look and Listen". If in some way we could make it compulsory for vehicles to come to a complete stop at level crossings, and if it were properly controlled, it would solve the problem to a great extent, because in time people would become educated to it and the majority would come to a full stop. It would prevent a great many fatal accidents and a great deal of the damage to property.

maintopic: ASKING OF QUESTIONS ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN ANNUAL APPROPRIATION TO GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
I wish to say just a few words on this matter. It has been discussed by hon. members from nearly every point in Canada

Railway Act
except my own province. It is not necessary for me to say that we have the same problem in New Brunswick as other provinces have. As a matter of fact between Moncton and Saint John there are probably as many grade crossings as, if not more than, there are in any other part of Canada.
I was much interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Waterloo North, who mentioned the protection that is given in other countries. Many of us will remember that in England 40 years ago there were very few level crossings. They had overhead bridges and underpasses in practically every part of the country where there was a railway crossing. Forty years ago they were that far ahead, and I have often wondered why we have been so slow in Canada.
I agree with other hon. members that $5 million a year is very little as far as the elimination of railway crossings in this country is concerned. We certainly should have the $33 million a year which was recommended by the commission. The sum of $33 million spent over the years would place us in a position comparable with that of other countries.
I agree with the hon. member for York West, who pointed out that the federal government collects hundreds of millions of dollars from the automobile industry in this country. There is no reason why this money should not be spent to make the roads safer for the automobile owners and users of the
roads. The provinces collect money from the automobile industry for the upkeep of roads. Apart from helping to construct the trans-Canada highway, on which they are spending something like $15 million a year, the federal government makes no other contribution to the upkeep of roads.
Since it is now nearly ten o'clock I shall not say anything else on this matter tonight, but I endorse what has been said by all hon. members. I do not think the amount provided for in this legislation will be enough to do the job. Something further must be done for the protection of the public so far as railroad crossings are concerned.
